blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

I first saw The House Is Black as a teenager in Iran, on a copy of a copy, in a room where we were not supposed to be watching it. It is twenty-two minutes long. I lasted most of it, and what I felt was not admiration. I was frightened, and underneath the fright, which is harder to write down, I was disgusted. I remember wanting it to stop and I remember being ashamed of wanting that even while I wanted it.
It took me a long time to understand that this reaction was the film working exactly as she intended, and that I had failed a test she had set on purpose.

Forough Farrokhzad went to a leprosy colony near Tabriz in 1962 and stayed twelve days, at a time when nobody touched those people and nobody looked at them and the official position of the civilised world was that they should be somewhere else. She filmed them eating, praying, playing ball, marrying, having their beards trimmed and their wounds dressed. She filmed a classroom. She refused, absolutely and throughout, to let their faces be the whole of what they were. And she came out with a child, whom she raised.
She was thirty-two when she died, five years later, on a road outside Tehran.

What she did in those twenty-two minutes is the thing this imprint exists to do, and I want to say so plainly rather than leave it as an influence in a list. She took a group of people whose appearance made them unbearable to look at, and therefore unbearable to hear, and she made a piece of work that forced the looking and then, having forced it, made the looking beside the point. That is the whole trick and almost nobody manages it. Most attempts either flinch or wallow. She did neither. She held the camera exactly still and let a woman look at herself in a mirror for eleven seconds longer than anyone wants, and by the end of it you are no longer looking at a disease.

Every book I have published under this number and the sixty-two before it has been an attempt at the same manoeuvre with different material. The unheard are not usually silent. They are usually unpleasant to attend to, for reasons of smell or grammar or damage or shame, and the world's indifference to them is not cruelty so much as flinching — the ordinary, automatic, physical pulling-away that a body does when something arrives it does not want. That flinch is the subject of this entire series. It happens to be, also, the medical fact at the bottom of this book, which is not a coincidence I planned and which I noticed only after the structure was built.

Leprosy is not a rotting disease. That is folklore and it is wrong. It kills the nerve, and everything that follows — the ruined hands, the blindness, the shortened fingers — happens because a body stopped sending word and its owner could not be warned. It is a disease of not feeling. I have spent a year now with the thought that the people we cannot bear to look at have, in that specific sense, less of a problem than we do.
I want to be exact about what is invented here, because the real people are owed that.

The colony in these pages is not Baba Baghi. The filmmaker is not Forough. The child is not the boy she adopted, who is alive, who has a name and a life and a profession of his own, and who has never been anything other than a man and certainly not a device in somebody's novella. The conspiracy at the centre of this book did not happen. Nobody rationed anybody's medicine. There was no register.

What is true is the disease, the arithmetic of the graveyard, the fact that the cure has existed cheaply since the 1940s, and the fact that these places went on existing anyway, for decades, because it was easier for everybody outside the wall not to look.
She looked. As a frightened teenager in a room where we should not have been, I did not, and it has taken me most of my life to grow into the mind that made that film.
This one is hers.
Chew Z
PART ONE — THE STAGING
THE COLD ROOM
I came here for the faces.
Let that be written somewhere honest,
in the ledger where they keep my name and my permit.
I have a hunger with beautiful manners.
I have twelve days
and a house that has been waiting
longer than I have been alive.

The building I work in was a customs shed until 1974 and it has never entirely stopped being one. You can still see where the freight doors were bricked up, a slightly different red, like a scar that healed under supervision. On the ground floor a man restores municipal footage — parades, dredging, the mayor cutting things — and on the second floor there is me, and a Steenbeck flatbed the colour of a hospital, and four hundred cans of other people’s memory in a room I keep at fifteen degrees.

Everybody in this trade develops a private way of describing what we do. The Belgians say they are washing film. My predecessor said he was a dentist. I have never had a phrase for it, which I used to think was a failure of imagination and now understand differently.
What I do is sit still and look at one frame for a long time.

That is the entire job. A frame is a photograph that lasts one twenty-fourth of a second and was never meant to be looked at, and if you look at it long enough it stops being part of a film and becomes a room you can walk around in. You see the boom shadow. You see the extra in the third row who is not acting. You see that the light has moved four inches between two shots that are supposed to be continuous, which means somebody broke for lunch, which means somebody lied.

I can do this for eight hours. The others cannot. Willem gets up every eleven minutes; I have counted, not out of cruelty but because counting is also a thing I can do for eight hours. He walks to the window, he touches the radiator, he comes back. He has a body that keeps sending him messages and he answers all of them, every time, the way a man answers a telephone in an empty house because he cannot bear the noise.
I used to be quietly, stupidly proud of this. I thought it was character.

In March I burned my forearm on the lamp housing of the Steenbeck and did not know until Els asked me at dinner what I had done to my arm. There was a mark on it the length of a matchstick, a good clean burn, already blistered, and I looked at it the way you look at a coat someone has left on your chair. It belonged to somebody. I had been wearing it for perhaps four hours.

Els is a sound editor. She is Dutch to a degree that people from Utrecht find excessive. She said, you did not feel that, not as a question, and I said something about being absorbed in work, and she let it go, because we have been married sixteen years and she knows which of my doors are painted on.

The mark healed. What did not heal was the patch around it, which is the size of a playing card and lies on the outside of the left forearm, and which is not numb in the way a foot is numb. A foot going numb announces itself. This does not announce anything. If I close my eyes and Els draws on that patch with the tip of a pen, I know she is there, I can feel the pressure, I simply cannot feel what. Hot, cold, sharp, blunt — the arm has opinions on all four and declines to share them. It has gone discreet.
That was three months ago. I have told no one. I have looked it up in one library, in a language I read badly, on purpose.
And I have been running the reels every night since.

There are eleven cans. They came to me in 1975, through a lawyer in Tehran and then a lawyer in Paris and then a woman at a festival who handed them over in the bar of a hotel and said, these are yours, apparently, in a tone that suggested she had expected me to be more grateful. I was nineteen. I put them in a cupboard for six years.

Nine of the cans are the finished film. Two are trims — the cuttings, the discards, the material that lost. Everybody who has ever heard about the trims has assumed they are worthless, and until March I was one of them.
I want to be precise about what I was doing in March, because I have gone back over it many times and I still cannot find the moment where I decided.
I did not decide. I went numb, and I went to the reels.

It was not a plan. It was closer to what a dog does when it is unwell, which is to go and lie in the one place it associates with safety and stay there without knowing why. My arm stopped reporting and I climbed the stairs to the cold room and threaded the first can, and the flatbed made its noise like a lift descending, and I sat down in front of forty minutes of black-and-white that I have known since I was nineteen and could describe frame by frame with my eyes shut.
And I began, without instruction, to look for something.

I have thought about that more than I have thought about the arm. Because a man who finds a numb patch on his body goes to a doctor. That is what the interruption is for. That is the whole design — you are hurt, the body screams, you attend to it, you live. It is the oldest arrangement in the world and it is very nearly the definition of being alive.
I did not go to a doctor. I went upstairs, in the dark, alone, and sat perfectly still in front of the only object I own from before, and started looking for the reason.
At the time I thought this was grief, or vanity, or the ordinary morbid curiosity of a man turning forty in a wet city.
I know now it was obedience.
ELEVEN KILOMETRES
The road ends and then continues badly
the way a sentence continues after the truth in it.
There is no sign for where I am going.
The men who drew the map were told the place exists
and were not told what it is called,
and so they left a thumbprint of white
and went home to their wives.
The road is good for eleven kilometres.

Parvaneh Kamrani notices the precise point at which it stops being good, because she is sitting in the back of a hired Jeep with a Bolex in her lap and nothing to do but notice things. The metalled surface simply ends, mid-slope, without warning or barrier, the way a man stops talking when he decides he has said enough. After that it is graded dirt, then track, then two pale lines in the scrub where vehicles have been before but not lately.
‘Someone paid for eleven kilometres,’ she says.

Jalil is in front with the driver and does not turn round. He is twenty-six and has been hired for eleven days and is already regretting eight of them. ‘Someone paid for a photograph of eleven kilometres,’ he says.
She writes that down. She writes everything down; it is the only discipline she has ever kept.

They come over the rise at four in the afternoon and the House is below them in a shallow bowl of ground, and she puts her hand on the driver’s shoulder to stop the car without saying anything, and gets out, and stands in the road.
It is smaller than she expected and much more beautiful, and both of these facts make her feel obscurely cheated.

A wall of mud brick the colour of weak tea, half a mile around, low enough to see over from up here. A line of poplars along the northern edge, planted decades ago by somebody who thought about shade, throwing long moving stripes across the roofs. Whitewash inside — everything whitewashed, walls, doorframes, the low kerbs of the paths, so white in the afternoon that it hurts to look at directly. Smoke from the kitchen. Two women crossing a yard with a basket between them. A dog.

It looks like a village. That is what she will say later, to everyone, for the rest of her life: it looks like a village, it looks like any village in the country, that is the first cruelty, that they gave it the shape of a place where people simply live.
‘Get this,’ she says.
Jalil gets it. Four hundred feet, from up on the rise, the whole bowl in one static frame with the poplars moving. It will be the second shot in the finished film and it will be on the poster.
‘They know we are coming?’ he says.
‘They have known for six weeks.’
‘They agreed?’
She looks at him. Jalil has the face of a man who wants to be told the arrangement is clean, and she has not been able to give anyone that face for a long time now.
‘A committee agreed,’ she says. ‘In an office. With a stamp.’

The gate is wood, and old, and standing open. There is a painted board above it with the Ministry’s designation — STATION NINE — and underneath, in smaller letters, the word that the Ministry uses in its correspondence and that she has been careful not to say aloud since Tehran.
Nobody is waiting for them.

This throws her more than a delegation would have. She had prepared herself for hostility and prepared herself for gratitude, and had rehearsed a small speech for each, and what she gets is a hot empty yard, a dog that does not get up, and the sound of somebody sweeping out of sight.
They stand in it for four minutes with the camera and the cases.

Then a woman comes out of the school with an exercise book under her arm and walks across the yard towards them without hurrying, and this is Ozra, though Parvaneh will not learn her name for another hour and will not spell it correctly in her notes for three days.

She is perhaps fifty. She has no eyebrows. Parvaneh registers this and registers her own registering of it, the small internal lurch, the flinch she has promised herself she will not perform, and she is so busy managing her own face that she almost misses the fact that Ozra has stopped four feet away and is looking at her with what can only be described as patience.
‘You are the guest,’ Ozra says.
Mehmān [meh-MAAN]. The ordinary word. Guest, visitor, the one who is received.
‘I am Parvaneh Kamrani. This is Jalil. We are —’

‘You are the guest,’ Ozra says again, agreeably, as though correcting a child’s arithmetic without embarrassing it, and turns and starts walking, and they follow her, and Parvaneh writes in her notebook that evening: they are a hospitable people, formal, they use the polite forms.
Thirty-four years later a man in a cold room in Rotterdam will run that reel and hear the word and think nothing of it either, for eleven more months.
WHAT YOU REMEMBER
Forty minutes.
Ten thousand people have wept in the dark at it
and gone out into the street afterwards
and eaten something,
and told a friend they must see it,
and slept well.
This is not their fault.
I built it to do that.
You have probably seen the film.

I say that without vanity, since I had nothing to do with making it and everything to do with being in it. It runs forty minutes. It has been in the Sight and Sound lists twice. It plays at retrospectives in cities where nobody can find the country on a map, and it is taught in schools in three languages, and there is a print in a vault in Belgium that is rated to survive most things a building can do.
If you have seen it, here is what you remember.

You remember the opening, which is a woman at a mirror. It is a small mirror with flowers painted round the frame, propped on a shelf at the wrong height, and she is looking into it and adjusting her headscarf. She has no nose. There is an opening in the middle of her face where the bridge came down, and one of her eyes has gone white, and she does not blink, and the shot is held eleven seconds longer than you want it to be held.
That is the first thing that happens, and it is the reason people talk about the film in the tone they use.

You remember the boy who says the prayer — the ordinary child’s prayer of thanks, for hands to work with, for eyes to see with — recited in a flat little voice to somebody off camera, while the hands he is thanking God for lie curled in his lap like two things asleep.

You remember the classroom, obviously. Everybody remembers the classroom. The teacher asking them to name beautiful things, and the answers coming in the way children answer, competitively, all of them at once — the moon, the sun, flowers, playtime — and then the same teacher asking them to name ugly things, and the pause, and a small boy at the front saying: hand. Foot. Head.
You remember the man on crutches at the end coming straight at the lens until he blacks out the frame.
You remember the gate closing.

What you probably do not remember, because it lasts nine seconds, is a child of five or six being carried across the corner of a shot on somebody’s shoulder, out of focus, in the direction of the bathhouse.
That’s me.

I have watched this film since I was nineteen. It would be reasonable to assume I watched it in the way an orphan reads a birth certificate, which is what I told the two women I was involved with in my twenties, both of whom were very moved and neither of whom asked a follow-up question. It made a good story. It made me interesting in the specific way that a young man in Europe with a bad history is interesting, and I traded on it, and if there is a small crime at the bottom of my life it is that one and it is not the one I am writing about.

She gave me a name out of a book, which is what you do when a child arrives without one. Dariush. I have had it thirty-four years and it has never once felt like a thing I was called rather than a thing I answered to, and I did not understand why until this year.
The truth is duller and worse.
I watched it looking for my mother’s face.

Not out of longing. I have never had a single memory of the place — nothing, not a smell, not a doorway, and I have tested this repeatedly and unkindly. I was five. Nothing came out with me. So there was no longing available, and what I had instead was arithmetic: there are two hundred and ten people in that colony and roughly ninety of them appear in the film and one of them made me, and I have forty minutes of black-and-white in which to work out which.
I did that for eleven years. Every woman’s face, frame by frame, in the cold room, on the flatbed, with the sound off.
I never found her.
I want you to hold on to that, because it is the piece I cannot forgive, and I will be coming back to it.
She is in the film. She is in it for eleven minutes, uninterrupted, alone in the frame, talking directly into the lens.
I looked at her, at four frames a second, more times than I can count, and I did not know, and there was no reason on earth I should have known.

But she knew. She is looking at the camera because she is looking at me. She is speaking to a room she will never see, in a city she cannot imagine, thirty-four years in front of her, and she is telling me the one thing that would have saved all of us.
And it is subtitled, in every print, in every language, as a prayer.
NO CORNERS
There is not one sharp corner in this place.
I have gone round with my hand out like a blind woman
touching the doorframes, the tables, the lip of the water,
and every edge has been taken off by somebody
patiently, over years, with a rasp.
I came to film the ruined.
They have built the gentlest room on earth
and I cannot make my hand stop shaking.
By the end of the second day she has three pages and none of it is what she came for.

Whitewash. Everything, twice a year, inside and out, walls and kerbs and doorframes and the stones round the water. She had assumed poverty — the same cheap lime over everything because there is nothing else. It is not that. She asks a man refilling a bucket why and he says, without looking up: so that a mark shows.
She does not understand this for another two days and when she does understand it she has to leave the yard.

Corners. There are none. Not on any doorframe, not on the tables in the kitchen, not on the low walls, not on the stone channel that brings the stream down through the middle of the compound, whose lips have been worked round by hand, unhurriedly, across years, so that the whole watercourse has the soft shoulders of something in a bathhouse. Nowhere in this village is there a right angle at the height of a hip. You could walk the entire place blindfold and not take a cut.
She writes: they have made it safe for people who cannot be warned.
Then she crosses it out, because it is too neat, and she has a horror of the too neat, and she writes it again underneath anyway.
Sound. This is the one that gets under her, and it takes her until the third day to find the words, and it is Jalil who finds them first, standing in the yard at dusk with the camera down.
‘Nobody drops anything,’ he says.

He is right. In an ordinary village there is a constant low percussion running under everything — a cup set down badly, a coin, a knife on a board, the small clatter of objects being fumbled and caught by hands that know they can catch. Here that sound does not exist. Objects are placed. Two hands, always, and set down flat, and released deliberately, and the release is a separate action from the placing. She watches an old man put a glass on a table with the care of a man defusing it.
A hand that cannot feel cannot catch.

So there is no percussion, and the absence of it gives the whole House the manner of a church, and the effect on a visitor is not peace. The effect is a low continuous alarm that she cannot locate the source of. She sleeps badly for eleven nights and blames the mattress.
The graveyard. They pass it on the way to the shrine and she asks, idly, how many people live in the House.
‘Two hundred and ten,’ Ozra says.

Parvaneh looks at the graveyard, which is the size of a football pitch and full, and does the arithmetic while she is walking, and it comes out and lands in her, and she keeps walking and says nothing, and Ozra says nothing either, and lets her carry it.
She will think about that silence a great deal in the years afterwards. She will decide it was tact.
The money. On the second morning she is shown the tokens, and this is the first thing in the House that delights her, in the shameful greedy way that a good detail delights a person who makes films.

They mint their own coin. Aluminium, light as a bottle cap, stamped with a crescent on one side and a number on the other. It has existed for thirty years, since the disease was believed to travel out on cash, and the belief was wrong, and the coin was struck anyway and never withdrawn. They buy bread with it. They pay each other with it. The boys gamble with it against the school wall.
Eleven kilometres up that road it is worth precisely nothing.
‘And this?’ she says, turning one over. ‘Two thousand and six?’
‘That is not the value,’ says Ozra.
‘What is it?’
Ozra takes the coin back from her, gently, with two hands, the way everything is taken and given in that place, and puts it in her pocket.
‘A number,’ she says.
THE SECOND TAKE
Somebody has moved the sun.
Between the second shot and the third
the shadow of the poplar has walked four inches west
and a woman has changed her mind about being filmed
in a light that arrived an hour later.
Grief does not keep to a schedule.
Only work does.
I found the first one on the ninth of April, at about two in the morning, and I have the date because I wrote it on the can label before I understood why I would want it.

It is not a discovery in any dramatic sense. It is the dullest thing in the world and any competent restorer would have caught it, and the only reason nobody has is that nobody has ever had a reason to run the trims and the finished film against each other on the same bench, frame by frame, at four frames a second, in the middle of the night, in March, with an arm that has stopped reporting.
Here is what is in the film.

Reel one, second minute. Parvaneh and Jalil arrive in the yard and begin to set up and a man comes out of a doorway and refuses to be filmed. He is perhaps sixty. He puts his hand up — a curled hand, the fingers drawn in — and says no, twice, and turns his back and goes in, and the camera keeps running for a beat too long on the empty doorway.
It is a famous nine seconds. It is quoted in essays. It is the moment the film declares its ethics: we are not entitled to these people, and here is the proof, we left it in.
Then, forty seconds later, a woman comes out of the same doorway and stands and lets them film her, and does not speak, and the film has begun.
In the trims, the same man refuses in the same doorway, in the same clothes, with the same hand.
And the shadow of the poplar across the door is four inches west.

I sat with that for a long time. There is a very ordinary explanation and I went and got it and held it up: film is expensive, light changes, a cameraman with eleven days and a limited stock might well ask a man who has already refused to refuse again, later, in better light, and no honest person would call that a lie.
Except that the man’s second refusal is better.

Not different. Better. The hand comes up a fraction earlier and stays up a fraction longer. The turn is cleaner. The head is angled so that the light gets the side of the face where the damage is, which it does not in the first take. In the first take he mumbles the second no. In the second take he does not.
He got a note. Somebody gave that man a note between takes, and it was a good note, and he took it well.
I checked the woman who follows him. Two takes. The second one better.
I checked everything in the first four minutes.

By the middle of April I had found eleven separate setups in the trims that exist twice, and in every single case the version in the finished film is the second one, and in every single case the second one is stronger. Not stronger in the sense of better photographed. Stronger in the sense of better performed.

Somewhere around the fifteenth I stopped and made myself say the whole thing out loud in the cold room, because there is a discipline in this work about not letting a theory live in your head where it can grow in the dark.
The most celebrated act of restraint in the history of the documentary — the refusal that the filmmaker left in to show she knew she was an intruder — was rehearsed.
Not by her.

I got Jalil’s number from the back of a Dutch festival catalogue in a library in Amsterdam. He had given a talk in 1988 and the organiser had printed his address, which is the kind of carelessness that no longer happens and which I have benefited from twice in my life.
He answered on the fourth ring. Seventy-eight, and the voice was thirty years younger than the man.
I said who I was. There was a silence of about four seconds, which is a very long silence on a telephone, and then he said, in Persian, in a completely different register:
‘You are the boy.’
‘Yes.’
‘What took you.’

Not a question. He did not ask it as a question. Thirty-four years, and the first thing that came out of him was mild professional impatience, the tone of a man who has been sitting in a waiting room since 1962 and is now being seen.
‘I have some questions about the arrival footage,’ I said.
‘Yes,’ said Jalil. ‘Of course you do. Come to Cologne. Not on the telephone, and not because of the police. Because I am old and I will need to see your face when I tell you.’
THE LOOKING
At the bell they come out into the last of the light
and take each other’s feet into their laps.
I have never been touched like that.
Not by my mother, not by either husband,
not by the man I ruined myself for
in the summer I do not write about.
They are looking for stones and small openings.
It is the tenderest thing I have ever filmed
and I am so lonely I could put my face in the dirt.

The bell goes at sundown and it is not a religious bell. It is a school bell on an iron bracket by the kitchen door, and a boy rings it by pulling a cord, and it is the only sharp sound in the whole of the House.
Two hundred doors open.

Parvaneh is standing in the middle of the main path with a light meter in her hand when it happens and she has no warning of it, and she turns on the spot, once, all the way round, and Jalil — who has been half asleep against a wall — is on his feet with the Bolex before she has finished turning, which is the only reason the sequence exists.
They come out and sit down in pairs.

On the low walls, on the steps, on the kerbs, in the last twenty minutes of usable light: two by two, all across the compound, unhurried, in a distribution so even that it can only be habit and looks from a distance like choreography. Husbands and wives. Two old men. A woman and a girl. Two boys, sniggering, being told to sit properly by somebody’s mother.
And then they take off their shoes and begin to go over each other.

It is done in a fixed order and Parvaneh will not work out the order until Day Six. Feet first, always. One person takes the other’s foot into their lap and goes over it with their eyes four inches away — sole, heel, the sides, between each toe, the skin behind the ankle — and then turns the shoe over and shakes it out and runs a finger round the whole inside of it. Then the other foot. Then the hands, palm and back and the web between each finger. Then the forearms. Then the face, which is done with a small mirror if the pair are equally sighted and with fingertips if they are not.
Then somebody counts blinks. She thinks at first that this is a game.

There is talking throughout. Ordinary talking, gossip, complaint, a boy being asked about his arithmetic. Nobody is solemn. It has exactly the tone of a family shelling beans on a step, and it goes on for perhaps twenty-five minutes, and then the light goes and they get up and go in.
‘What is it called?’ she asks.
‘Negāh,’ says Ozra. [ne-GAAH]
The Looking. The plainest word in the language for it. To look at, to have a look, to keep an eye on.
‘Every evening?’
‘Every evening.’
‘For how long?’
Ozra considers this. ‘How long has anyone been alive here.’

Parvaneh films it on the second evening and again on the fourth and the seventh and the ninth, and it will be four and a half minutes in the finished film, and it is the material that everybody uses when they talk about the beauty of that House, and it is the reason the word tenderness attaches itself to a film about a leper colony and never comes off.

She has understood one thing correctly. She has understood that these people cannot be warned by their own bodies and so must be warned by each other, that the Looking is an entire civilisation’s answer to the problem of a silent nerve, and that a stone in a shoe left unfound will open a hole in a foot across a week and never once announce itself. All of that is true and she gets all of it, and she gets it in the first forty-eight hours, and it is the reason the film is great.
What she does not have is the boy.

He is in the sequence. He is in it on nine of the twelve evenings, and he is always in the fourth pair from the poplars, which is where the last of the light is and therefore where a cameraman with limited stock will point. He is five. He is passed from lap to lap across the twenty-five minutes — his feet done by one woman, his hands by another, his face by a third — which is how it is done with the small children, everybody says so, ask anyone, the little ones go round.
Four adults handle him on the second evening.
Three of them are among the worst cases in the House.
He is the only child in the compound who goes round.
PART TWO — THE RATION
COLOGNE
The old men who worked on the great cruel projects
are all living in small flats now
with a balcony and a plant they water on Sundays.
None of them are hiding.
That is the thing nobody tells you.
You knock, and they put the kettle on,
and they have been ready since before you were born.
Cologne in May, and the flat was on the fourth floor of a post-war block behind the station, the kind of building that was put up quickly by people who had recently learned what happens to buildings.
Jalil opened the door in a cardigan.

That is the detail I keep going back to. I had spent the entire train journey constructing him — I had him as a man with something to protect, a man who would need working on, and I had prepared four different approaches and discarded three of them somewhere around Duisburg. And what opened the door was a small tidy widower in a brown cardigan with reading glasses pushed up on his head, who looked at my face for slightly too long and then stood aside and said, ‘You have her hands.’
‘Whose?’

‘Parvaneh’s,’ he said. ‘You are holding the strap of your bag exactly the way she held the strap of her bag,’ and he went into the kitchen to deal with the kettle, and I stood in the hallway of a stranger’s flat in Germany and had to put my hand on the wall.

I want to record that he was kind. There is a version of this account in which the cameraman is a coward and an accomplice and I go at him for four hours and break him open. That version would be easier to read. What actually happened is that a decent, careful old man made tea and answered every question I asked as accurately as he could, and the accuracy was the injury, and by the end of the afternoon I wanted him to lie to me and he would not.

We did an hour of nothing first. His wife, dead in ’91. His son in Hamburg. My work, which interested him professionally — he wanted to know about the Steenbeck, he wanted to know what we were doing about vinegar syndrome, he asked two questions about my splicing that no one has asked me in eleven years.
Then he said: ‘You have found the doubles.’
Not a guess. He had put four decades between himself and that fortnight and he had never once stopped knowing precisely what was in the trims.
‘Eleven setups,’ I said.
‘There are nineteen.’
I had my notebook out and I did not write it down, which tells you something about the state I was in.
‘She knew?’

‘Parvaneh?’ He took his glasses off his head and cleaned them on the cardigan, which I came to understand was what he did instead of pausing. ‘She ordered half of them. That is the part you will not want. She was not deceived about the retakes. She was a filmmaker with eleven days and forty rolls of stock and a man who mumbled his line, and she said, again, please, and this time do not swallow the second no, and she said it in front of me, and I turned over, and it is completely ordinary. Every documentary you have ever loved has that in it.’
‘And the other half?’
Jalil put his glasses back on.
‘The other half we did not order,’ he said. ‘The other half were offered.’

He said it happened first on the second morning. A woman had done a scene in the kitchen doorway, one take, perfectly good, and Parvaneh had thanked her and moved on. And an hour later the woman came and found Jalil where he was changing a magazine and said, in Azeri, that she had done it wrong and would do it again now, and did it again, and it was better.
‘And you filmed it.’

‘I filmed it. I was twenty-six and I had stock and a woman was standing in good light asking me to. What would you have done?’ He shrugged, and it was not a defensive shrug. ‘By the fourth day it happened perhaps twice a day. We started to enjoy it. We said to each other: they have understood cinema. We were extremely pleased with ourselves.’
‘Who was giving the notes?’
He was quiet for a while.

‘There was a woman called Ozra who taught the children,’ he said. ‘She was never once in front of the camera. Not one frame. I have looked. You will look too and you will not find her either.’ He turned his cup round on the saucer. ‘She used to stand behind me. Not in the way that people stand behind a camera to see what you are seeing. Behind my shoulder, at about here’ — he touched the back of his neck — ‘and she never spoke while we turned over. Not once in twelve days. And afterwards she would say something to somebody in Azeri, three or four words, and walk off.’
‘You didn’t have the Azeri.’
‘I had perhaps a third of it. I am from Isfahan, boy. I had a third of it on a good day and none of it when they were quick.’
‘And Parvaneh?’
‘None. Not a word. She had the Persian and she was very proud of her ear and she had none of it at all.’
He got up then and went to the balcony door and stood looking at somebody’s washing, and I let him, and when he spoke again the register had changed.
‘We were told what was said,’ Jalil said. ‘That is the thing. We did not go untranslated. Somebody stood next to us for twelve days and told us what was being said.’
‘Who?’
‘Ozra,’ he said. ‘She had beautiful Persian. She translated everything.’
THE WOMAN WHO MOVES
The water comes down out of the hills and through the middle of the
village
and every stone along its lip has been made kind by hand.
A boy runs past me with his arms out
and I flinch for him the whole length of the yard.
Nobody else does.
They are watching him with the calm of people at a harbour
who know exactly how deep the water is.
Day Three, and the House lets her in a little.

This is not a decision anybody announces. It is simply that on the third morning there are more doors open than there were, and a woman she has not spoken to says good morning to her by name, and when she sets the camera up by the water channel three boys come and stand in shot on purpose and have to be shooed, giggling.
She films the stream for most of the morning. It is the closest thing to a holiday she has had in two years.

The channel runs the length of the compound and it is the reason anyone chose this bowl of ground in the first place. It comes down off the hills cold and clean, and it has been given a stone bed, and the stone has been worked. She goes along the whole run of it with her hand out, touching, the way you would run a hand along a rail. Every lip rounded. Every corner taken off. Where the channel passes the bathhouse somebody has set two flat stones as a step and the edges of both have been rasped down to a curve.
‘How long does that take?’ she asks. ‘To do all of it.’
‘Which of us?’ says the man she has asked, who is a carpenter and who has three fingers on his left hand and holds a rasp with a leather cuff strapped round the palm.
‘Anyone.’
‘Forty years,’ he says. ‘On and off.’

She writes it down and underlines it and, later, in Tehran, in an editing room, at four in the morning, she will read that line in her own handwriting and start crying so hard that the assistant will go out and stand in the corridor.

The boys play against the school wall with the tokens. Pitch and toss, and the game is old and universal and would be identical in any yard in the world, and she films four minutes of it and cuts it to eleven seconds. What she does not catch — because she is at the wrong angle and because she is watching the coins — is that one of the boys is holding his hand out flat to be looked at by another boy between throws, without either of them breaking off the argument they are having.
There is a woman in the yard that morning who does not come near her.

Parvaneh notices her because she is the only adult in the compound who has actively arranged her day around not being in shot. Everyone else has settled somewhere on the scale between shy and delighted. This one moves. When the camera goes to the north side she is on the south side. When they set up by the kitchen she goes to the water.
‘Who is that?’
‘That is Sanam,’ Ozra says.
‘She doesn’t want to be filmed.’
‘No.’
‘I’d like to talk to her.’
‘You may talk to anyone,’ says Ozra. ‘They are not mine.’

Parvaneh goes over at midday. Sanam is washing something in the channel and does not look up. She is perhaps thirty, which in that place makes her young, and her hands are far gone — both of them, the fingers drawn in tight to the palms — and she is managing the washing with her wrists and forearms in a way that is so practised it takes Parvaneh a moment to see that the hands are not being used at all.
‘Peace be upon you,’ Parvaneh says, in Persian.
Sanam looks up.

What happens next is nine or ten seconds long and Parvaneh writes three different accounts of it in three different years and never gets it to sit still. The woman looks at her. Not with hostility. Not with the shyness she has had from a dozen others. She looks at Parvaneh the way you look at a road you have been told to expect, and then she says one sentence in Azeri, quite fast, and goes back to the washing.
Parvaneh does not have Azeri.
She goes and finds Ozra by the school and repeats the sentence phonetically, badly, and Ozra listens with her head slightly tilted.
‘She says she is not well today,’ Ozra says.
‘That’s all?’
‘That is all.’

And Parvaneh writes in her notebook: S. — unwell, hostile? — try again later, and does try again, twice, on Day Six and Day Nine, and gets her on Day Nine, and it is eleven minutes long, and it is the only interview in the film that Ozra does not translate.
GOOD NEWS
The doctor is a kind man in a kind room
and he has good news for me,
and he says it twice
the way you say a thing to a child at a window
who has stopped listening
because outside, on the grass,
something is being buried.
The consultant was thirty-five at most and he had the manner they teach them now, which is to sit at the corner of the desk rather than behind it, and he was so pleased.

That is not sarcasm. He was genuinely, professionally pleased, and I have thought about him often since with something close to affection, because he was the last person to be in a room with me while my life still had the ordinary shape.
He said the name of it. Then he said, immediately, before I could do anything with my face: ‘This is completely curable.’
Then he said it again, in Dutch, slightly slower, and then he said it a third time in English, and I understood that he had been taught to do this because of what the word does to people.
Here is what he told me over about forty minutes, and I am setting it down plainly because it took me three months to stop rearranging it into something more dramatic.

It is a bacterium. It is very old and very slow and it has almost no interest in most of us — nineteen people out of twenty are simply immune, born that way, and will never catch it no matter what they do. It is not carried in a touch. It needs years of close living, the same air, the same bedding, the same small rooms, over and over, and even then it usually fails.

It does not rot anything. That is folklore and it is a thousand years old and it is wrong. Nothing dissolves. Nothing drops off in the night. What it does is go into the nerves — the long wires that run from the skin to the brain — and kill the wire. Not the hand. The wire.
So the hand stays. The hand works. The hand simply stops sending word.
‘And everything else,’ the consultant said, ‘follows from that.’

He drew it for me on a pad, which I did not need but did not stop. The burn you do not pull away from. The stone in the shoe you walk on for a week. The fingers that shorten across years — not eaten, he was very clear about that, but worn back, injury after unnoticed injury, the bone quietly giving up ground each time. The eye that stops closing because the wire to the lid has gone, so a person stops blinking and does not know it, and the eye dries and clouds from the middle outward across months, and there is no pain at any point in that process, not one moment of it, and then they are blind.
‘People go blind,’ I said, ‘from not blinking.’
‘Yes.’
‘That’s the whole mechanism.’

‘That is the whole mechanism,’ he said. ‘Which is why it is such good news that we found yours early. You have one patch. Everything after this is prevention. You will take three drugs for a year and you will be fine and you will keep your hands.’
He asked whether I knew where I had contracted it.
I said I had been born in a colony and taken out at five.

And his whole face changed — not to pity, to something better and much worse, which was a kind of historical embarrassment. He said, carefully, that the treatment I would start on Monday had existed since the 1940s. Cheap. By mouth. Reliable. That the reason places like the one I was born in still existed into the sixties was almost never medicine. It was money, and administration, and the fact that nobody wants to look.
‘It was available,’ I said.
‘It was available.’
‘In the forties.’
‘Yes.’
I thanked him, and shook his hand, and went down in the lift, and stood outside on the Schiedamsedijk in the rain for about twenty minutes.

Because I was thinking about a locked cabinet in a clinic in a bowl of ground eleven kilometres past the end of the road, which is in the film, which is on screen for nineteen seconds, in reel four, and which I have looked at perhaps three hundred times.
And I was thinking that I had never once asked myself what was in it.

I did not tell Els that night. I have gone over this and I cannot make it come out as anything other than what it is. I had a curable disease, a good prognosis, and a wife who is better at difficulty than I am, and I went home and ate a meal and did not say the word.
I started the drugs on the Monday and hid the boxes in a camera case.
I have since had a great deal of time to consider why, and the honest answer is not shame and it is not fear of losing her.
I did not want to be a patient.
BREAD
The bread is put into the oven by a woman
whose hands closed years ago
like two flowers deciding against it,
and she is faster than my mother was.
I have filmed her for six minutes.
When I look at what I have,
I find I have filmed only the hands
and cannot tell you one thing about her face.
The kitchen is the warmest room in the House and the only one with a right angle in it, which is the oven mouth, and there is a wooden guard fixed across the lower half of that.
Day Four. She spends nearly all of it in there.

Three women and a boy work the ovens from before dawn: two hundred and ten people, plus the school, plus whatever goes to the clinic, and the flour comes up from the town on a Tuesday. The senior of the three is called Golnaz, and Parvaneh films her for six minutes without moving the camera, and it is two minutes forty in the final cut, and it is the passage that people describe as unbearable.

Golnaz’s hands are closed. Both of them. The fingers have drawn in over about fifteen years until they lie against the palm, and the thumbs still work, and that is what she has: two thumbs and two padded fists and a pair of forearms she uses like tools. She takes the dough and turns it against the board with the heel of the hand. She lifts and slaps and folds. She is fast — Parvaneh times her against her own mother’s kitchen in her head and Golnaz is faster.
She does not look at what she is doing. She looks out of the window while she works, and talks, and laughs at something the boy says.
Then she stops, mid-sentence, and lifts her right forearm and turns it over and inspects the underside of it near the wrist, close, for about four seconds. Then she goes back to the dough.
Parvaneh does not ask about this until the evening, and when she does, Ozra says: ‘She smelled it.’
‘Smelled what?’

‘She goes past the oven mouth many hundreds of times a day,’ Ozra says. ‘She will not feel it. So she uses what she has. She smells her own arm cooking before she can see it. That is a skill. It took her four years and two bad ones to learn it and she is proud of it, and if you ask her she will tell you, and you should ask her, because she thinks you have only come to film what is missing.’

Parvaneh asks her. It is on the reel. Golnaz laughs and holds up the fist and turns it over and says something and everybody in the kitchen laughs, and it goes into the film untranslated, with no subtitle, because Ozra tells Parvaneh it is a joke about her husband.
Here is what else is in that day and is not in the film.

The boy is in the kitchen for a long stretch of the morning. He is five, and he is under everyone’s feet, and Golnaz gives him a piece of dough to work like every kitchen in the world gives a child a piece of dough to work. He is there when the bread comes out. He eats in the kitchen with the women rather than at the school, and Parvaneh, who has been in the House four days and has begun to relax, thinks this is charming.
He eats there every day. At the same time. Between the two firings, when all three women and the boy are in the same small hot room with the doors shut against the flies.
Ozra has never once been in the kitchen at that hour in twelve days.

She is in the school across the yard with her exercise book, and at eleven she looks up and out of the window, and if you slow reel three down to four frames a second you can see her do it, in the background of a shot of a dog, and the boy comes out of the kitchen forty seconds later.
TWO HUNDRED AND SIXTY-FOUR
A stamp, a date, a signature, a quantity.
A stamp, a date, a signature, a quantity.
Two hundred and sixty-four times,
and not one month missing,
and every hand that wrote them
went home afterwards to a good dinner
and slept beside somebody warm.

The Ministry of Health archive is in a basement in Tehran and I have never been in it. What I have is eleven weeks of correspondence, two hundred Deutschmarks to a researcher named Firouzeh who did the work properly and refused a bonus, and forty-one photocopies that arrived in a padded envelope in the second week of June.
They are supply records for Station Nine.

I had asked for something else. I had asked for the film permit, which is a different story and comes later. Firouzeh sent the permit and then sent a note saying that while she was in the box she had photographed the pharmacy schedules as well, because the box was thin and she was already there, and did I want them.
Two hundred and sixty-four monthly consignments. January 1940 to December 1961.
Not one gap.

I sat with those photocopies on the kitchen table for a long time, on a Sunday, with the children out, and I checked them against a table of doses that I had copied out of a library book in April and had not, until that morning, had any use for.

The colony had the cure from the beginning. The very beginning, the first years it existed anywhere in the world, delivered by cart and later by truck, monthly, uninterrupted, through a war and a coup and three ministers.
And it came in at roughly a fifth of what it should have been.
Not a tenth. Not a trace. A fifth is the important number, and it took me two more weeks and a second library to understand why, and when I understood it I had to go and stand in the garden.

A fifth is not neglect. Neglect looks like gaps. A fifth is not theft either; theft looks like a good month and then nothing. A fifth, delivered every single month for twenty-two years without one interruption, is a dose.

At that level the disease does not advance quickly. It also does not clear. People do not die of it in six years; they live with it for thirty, and the nerves go slowly, over decades, in the manner of something being negotiated rather than something being lost.
It preserves.

Someone worked that out. Somebody sat down with a table exactly like the one I copied in April and calculated the quantity at which two hundred and ten people would neither die nor recover, and then requisitioned that quantity every month for twenty-two years, and signed for it, and filed the counterfoil.
The signature on the receiving side is the same in nearly all of them. A physician’s registration number and a name I could not read for three days and then could: Meshkat.

The signature on the ordering side, on the requisition, is not a physician at all. It is a colony officer’s endorsement, which was procedurally required, and which in a place with no administration to speak of was given to whoever could write.
It is the same hand for twenty-two years. Small, upright, extremely regular, the handwriting of somebody who teaches children to write.
There is a version of me that got up from that table and went to the police, or to a newspaper, or on to an aeroplane.

What I actually did was go upstairs to the cold room and thread reel four and find the nineteen seconds of the clinic and run them back and forth, back and forth, until I could see the cabinet behind the doctor’s shoulder clearly enough to count the shelves.
Three shelves. Full.
And a woman in the queue in the foreground, waiting her turn, with her hand out.
THE CABINET
They stand in a line in the sun to be given something
and I have filmed the line
and I will call it patience,
and everyone who sees it will call it patience,
and there is a word in that language for what it actually is
and nobody will say it to me
for thirty-four years.
Dr Meshkat comes on the last Thursday of the month and he comes in a green Land Rover with a driver, and Day Four is a Thursday.

Parvaneh films the whole visit. It is the most conventional material she shoots in twelve days and she knows it, and she shoots it anyway because she has a producer in Tehran and a commissioning body called the Society for Assistance, and this is the footage that will make the case that money is required.
The queue forms at nine.

It runs from the clinic door down the length of the north path and there are perhaps ninety people in it, and it is entirely silent, and it does not move for the first forty minutes because the doctor is doing the bed cases first. Nobody complains. Nobody sits down, though there is a wall. They stand in the sun in a line with their hands at their sides and wait.
Inside, at a table by the window, Meshkat works fast and well.

He is fifty-odd and tired and not unkind. He does eleven examinations an hour. He has a nurse from the town with him and two of the residents assisting, and Parvaneh films him filing dead tissue from the sole of a man’s foot with an instrument like a rasp, calmly, the way a carpenter works a joint, while the man watches with interest and no expression at all and holds the leg steady himself.

She films a woman lying flat on a bench with her arms straight out while the nurse builds a stack of weighted pads across both hands. It looks, in the frame, exactly like a burial. It is in fact a good treatment, gentle and old and effective, and it will be in the film with no explanation and half the audiences in Europe will read it as a punishment.
And she films the cabinet.

It is behind Meshkat’s left shoulder for the whole of the clinic sequence: a metal press, painted the same white as everything, with three shelves visible through the glass and a lock. It is in shot for nineteen seconds in the finished film. She never asks about it. There is no reason on earth for her to ask about it; it is a medicine cabinet in a clinic, and there is a doctor standing in front of it, and the entire argument of the film she is making is that these people have been abandoned without treatment.
What she does ask, at the end of the day, standing outside while the Land Rover turns round in the yard, is what the queue was for.
‘The monthly,’ says Ozra.
‘They get it every month?’
‘Every month for as long as anyone here can remember.’
Parvaneh is aware of a small wrongness and cannot get at it, and she is tired, and the light has gone, and she has three hundred feet in the can that will move a committee to tears.
‘Then why is nobody better?’ she says.
And Ozra, who has answered every other question in four days immediately and in beautiful Persian, does not answer for a moment.
Then she says: ‘Because we are in the cold season.’
Parvaneh laughs, because it is April and warm, and takes it for what it plainly is — a country woman’s turn of phrase, fatalism, the kind of thing you write down and use later.
She does write it down. It is in the notebook, on the fourth page, in her hand.

Under it, that same night, she writes a line of verse, and thirty-four years later a man will find both on the same page and understand that she came within one question of the entire thing on the fourth day and asked something else instead.
PART THREE — THE QUIET
THREE AND A HALF MINUTES
They tell me about a garden.
All of them. The same garden.
Dry, with water down the middle
and something red at the far end.
I ask a blind man to describe the wall
and he describes my wall,
the one in the house where I was a girl,
and I write it down as folklore
because I am a coward with a notebook.
There is a stretch of the film that nobody writes about.

It runs from about nineteen minutes to twenty-two and a half, and every essay I have ever read on that film treats it as the low point — the passage where a great artist, exhausted at the halfway mark, put in some landscape. One critic in the seventies called it a breath. Another called it the film’s only lapse into the picturesque.
It is three and a half minutes of people sitting down.

There are eleven separate setups in it. An old man on a step against a whitewashed wall. Two women on a low bench with a basket between them that neither of them is doing anything with. A young man in a doorway. Somebody’s grandmother in the shade of the poplars. There is no dialogue and no narration over it and Parvaneh cut it against a single sustained note of a reed instrument that she recorded in the yard and slowed down.
The people in it are not asleep. Their eyes are open. They are not looking at anything.

I have run those three and a half minutes more than any other section of the film and until this year I would have told you exactly what the critics told you: rest, dignity, the poetry of ordinary time.
Here is what is actually in it.
In eleven setups over three and a half minutes, nobody moves.

I want to be exact about what I mean, because it sounds like nothing. Put a camera on a human being who is sitting still and doing nothing and time them. In a normal adult you will get, on average, something between four and nine seconds before something happens — a hand goes to the face, a foot changes its weight, the head resettles, somebody swallows and you see it, somebody scratches. This is not restlessness. This is the standard operating condition of the species. We are being spoken to constantly by our own skin and we answer every time, and we do it so continuously that we have no idea we are doing it, and it is the single hardest thing to fake in a performance. Directors know this. It is why still extras look dead.
The longest unbroken take in that sequence is fifty-one seconds. It is the old man on the step. In fifty-one seconds he blinks four times and does nothing else at all.
Not stillness in the sense of composure. Stillness in the sense of a photograph that somebody has left running.
I counted it eleven times, on eleven different people, across three and a half minutes of film, and the shortest of them is nineteen seconds and the average is a fraction over thirty.

And they are all doing something. That is the thing you can see once you know to look and can never unsee afterwards. It is not vacancy. There is a slight — I can only describe it as a lean. A very small forward attention, the face of a person listening to something at a distance in a language they know well.
Willem came in while I had the old man up on the bench in April and looked over my shoulder for a while.
‘What is he doing?’
‘I don’t know.’
‘He’s dead,’ Willem said, cheerfully, and went to the window, and touched the radiator, and came back.
Eleven minutes later he did it again. I timed it. I have timed him for years without ever once asking myself what the number meant.
THE WALL
A man walks the length of the wall with his hand out
and a voice recites the days of the week
over and over until they lose their edges
and become a kind of water.
I filmed him for ninety seconds
because I thought it was the saddest thing I had ever seen.
He was working.
I have never worked like that in my life.
Day Five, in the afternoon, in the flat white light after lunch when the House goes quiet, Parvaneh finds the blind man at the wall.

His name is Khodadad and he is somewhere past sixty and he has been blind for nine years. He walks the northern wall from the poplars to the corner and back, with his right hand out, the backs of the fingers just touching the whitewash, and he does it slowly, and he does it for a long time.
She sets up at the far end and lets it run. Ninety seconds, unbroken, no cut, the longest single take in the film.

Over it, in the finished version, there is a voice reciting the days of the week — Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday — around and around, flat, without inflection, until the words come apart. It is the most quoted thirty seconds she ever made. People write about it as an image of pure monotony, of time going nowhere in a place where nothing can change.
What is actually happening is this.
She asks Ozra, that evening, what he is doing out there.
‘Walking.’
‘For an hour?’
‘He does not know it is an hour,’ Ozra says.
‘Then what does he think it is?’
And Ozra looks at her for a moment and says: ‘Would you like me to ask him?’

They go out. He is still there. It is nearly dark. Ozra says something to him in Azeri and he laughs — a short surprised bark of a laugh — and answers at some length, and Ozra translates, and this is the exchange as Parvaneh records it in her notebook that night, and it is the exchange that later, in an editing room, she will decide is too oblique to use and will leave on the floor.
He says: tell her I am not walking, I am arriving.
He says: the wall is how I get out.
He says: I am sorry, it is not a thing that can be said in Persian.
Parvaneh writes underneath, in her own hand: Sufi? — ask O. tomorrow, gently. Query: is there an order here. Query: who leads it.

She does ask. What she gets, over the next three days, in pieces, is the first outline of the thing the House does not put in front of the camera because it does not occur to anyone that it would be of interest.
They call it khāmūshī [khaa-moo-SHEE]. The Quiet.

Ozra explains it the way you explain a local craft to a visitor — with a certain flatness, mild pride, no mysticism at all. Parvaneh, who has met a great many mystics in Tehran and has a low opinion of most of them, finds this reassuring and writes that down too.
The argument, as Ozra gives it, in the school room, in Persian, with the exercise books stacked between them:

Nobody outside this wall has ever held a single unbroken thought. Not one. In an entire life. The body will not permit it. You are interrupted every few seconds — an itch, a knee, a dry throat, a hand that wants to move — and you attend to it, always, immediately, without ever noticing that you have. You have never once been alone in a room with your own mind. You have only ever been in a room with your mind and something shouting at it.

And it is not the shouting that is the price, Ozra says. It is that a person who is interrupted every four seconds cannot go more than four seconds into anything. Not into a thought. Not into grief. Not into prayer. You live in a very shallow country and you have never seen the edge of it, and you believe the country is that size.
‘And here?’ Parvaneh says.
‘Here it went quiet,’ Ozra says. ‘And then we could hear how far it goes.’
‘That is a cruel bargain.’
‘Yes.’
‘And you would not undo it.’
Ozra stacks the exercise books, taps them square on the desk, sets them down with two hands.
‘You are asking whether I would like to be interrupted again,’ she says.
THE SAME GARDEN
He was a young man once
with a camera and a girl in Tehran
and eleven days of stock
and the whole thing in front of him,
and he says now that they were extremely pleased with themselves.
I would like to have known him then.
I would like to have known anybody then.
Second visit to Cologne, June, and this time I took the trims.

He had a projector. Of course he had a projector; he was eighty in a year and living alone and he had a 16mm projector on the sideboard the way other men that age have a fishing rod. We put a sheet up on the balcony door and ran the sit-still sequence twice, and then I ran the trims of it, which are nineteen minutes long.
Nineteen minutes. She shot nineteen minutes of people sitting down and cut three and a half.
Jalil watched it all the way through with his hands on his knees.
‘I remember the afternoon,’ he said. ‘I remember complaining. I said to her, we are burning stock on old men sleeping in the sun.’
‘What did she say?’

‘She said they are not sleeping.’ He took his glasses off and cleaned them on the cardigan. ‘She said it in a particular way. I did not follow it up, and I have thought since that this is the single largest failure of my professional life, and there is a lot of competition.’
I asked him what he had understood about the Quiet at the time.

‘Nothing. I did not know the word until you said it on the telephone.’ He said this without embarrassment. ‘You must understand what we thought we were doing, boy. We thought we were making an argument. The argument was: these people have been abandoned, this is curable, give money. That was the film. Everything that was not the argument was texture.’
‘She filmed nineteen minutes of texture.’
‘She filmed nineteen minutes of something she could not name and did not have room for,’ he said. ‘That is what a director’s floor is. It is all the things that were true and did not fit.’
Then he said: ‘Ask me about the garden.’
I had not mentioned a garden.
I want to set down precisely what happened in the room at that point, because it is the moment the ground moved and I have been careful with it since.
I said: what garden.

And Jalil said that on the sixth or seventh day he had been sitting on a step with a resident, waiting for the light, and had made conversation, and had asked the man — idly, with no interest, the way you ask anyone anything at four in the afternoon — where he went when he sat like that.
And the man had described a garden.

‘A walled garden,’ Jalil said. ‘Dry. Not green. Water down the middle in a stone channel and something red at the far end, a pomegranate, he said pomegranate. And I said, that is a nice garden, is it a garden you knew as a boy, and he said no. And I thought nothing of it whatsoever.’
He put his glasses back on.
‘And then two days later I asked a woman the same question because I had run out of things to say. And she described the same garden.’
‘The same.’
‘The channel. The pomegranate at the far end. The wall.’
‘They live together,’ I said. ‘They talk. It’s a story they tell each other, it’s a shared —’

‘Yes,’ said Jalil. ‘That is what I said to myself for thirty-four years and it is a perfectly good answer and I would like you to have it, and I am going to spoil it for you now because I am old and I have wanted to tell somebody this since 1962.’
He said the woman had told him where in the garden she stood.
Near the wall, on the left-hand side, she said. She had never gone past the water.

And Jalil, being twenty-six and bored and rather pleased with himself, had gone back to the first man on the following morning and had said: do you know so-and-so, and the man said yes. And Jalil said: where does she stand?
And the man said: near the wall on the left. She does not come past the water.
ELEVEN ANSWERS
There is a place they all go
and they can put each other in it
the way you put a chair in a room you know.
I asked what it looks like
and eleven people told me the same garden
and I wrote: shared folklore, cf. dream studies, ask Dr H.
I have been a coward in three languages.
Day Six. She spends it collecting descriptions and does not tell Jalil why.

She has a method for this, from journalism, from before: never ask two people in the same room, never repeat back what the last one said, never use a leading word. She asks eleven residents that day, singly, in the yard and the kitchen and the doorway of the bathhouse, one question in Persian with Ozra nowhere near her.
When you sit in the afternoon — where do you go?
Eleven answers. She numbers them in the notebook.

All eleven describe a walled garden. Nine of the eleven volunteer the watercourse without being asked. Seven volunteer the pomegranate. Two say only that there is something red at the end and they have never got close enough to see it.
Six of them place themselves in it — near the wall, by the water, at the shaded end — and four of the six name other residents and place them too. She cross-checks three of those. They agree.
She writes, that evening, in an entry that is still in the notebook and that I have photographed and have on my desk:

Not a vision. Nobody claims it is holy. Nobody claims it is God. They discuss it the way villagers discuss the road to the next town. O. says it is simply what is there when nothing else is. She will not say more and does not think it interesting. She thinks I am asking about it for the same reason a foreigner asks about carpets.
And underneath, in smaller writing, pressed harder:

Sensory work. They cannot feel their bodies. There is nothing coming in. So something comes out — brain filling silence, standard, I have read this. But then why the same garden. Eleven people. Why the same garden.
And then, right at the bottom of the page, six words:
Do not put this in the film.
She never wrote down her reason. I have thought about it for months.

The generous reading is that she was protecting them. She had come to make an argument that would loosen money out of a committee, and a colony of people who see a shared garden is a colony of mystics, and mystics do not get money, they get anthropologists.
The other reading is that she was frightened.

I incline to the second, and here is why. On the same page, in the same ink, she has written a line of verse that did not go into any collection and that I found nowhere else in her papers, and it reads:
I have asked eleven people where the wall is and they have all described my mother’s kitchen.
THE GUEST
Somebody stands behind them
and has stood there thirty years
and no one has turned in time.
They are not frightened of him.
They set a place.
When they call me guest
I thank them in the polite form
and go on believing
the word means me.
I am going to do this part badly. I have started it four times.
The medicine is straightforward and I want it on the table first, because it is the whole of the explanation and it explains nothing.

When the wires die, they do not go silent politely. They misfire. They send signal with no cause behind it — a burn where there is no fire, ants under skin that has nothing on it, and above all the sensation of being touched. This is ordinary and it is documented and it happens to people all over the world with damaged nerves, and the most common single form it takes is a hand laid flat on the body. Patients report it in hands they no longer have. It is not a mystery. It is a fault in a wire, and the brain, which cannot tolerate signal without a source, supplies one.
So: two hundred and ten people, in one enclosure, in partial permanent silence, in a state they have practised daily for thirty years, all of whom are periodically touched by nothing.
Of course they named it.
They call him mehmān [meh-MAAN]. The guest. The one who is received.

He stands behind you. He is always behind you, on the left, at about the height of a hand on a shoulder, and nobody in the history of that House has ever turned round in time. They are not afraid of him. This is the part I cannot make sit still. Every account Jalil has, every account in the trims, every account Firouzeh eventually turned up in a doctoral thesis from 1974 that nobody has cited since — they describe him without dread. Something between a lodger and a relative. Somebody who is simply in the house.
The children are taught not to try to turn round, because trying puts you out of the Quiet, and turning is what a body does when it is startled, and being startled is the outside world’s disease.
And Parvaneh Kamrani was called mehmān to her face, in Persian, by everybody in that compound, for twelve consecutive days.

I have gone back through the sound reels. It is there ninety-one times. Ozra says it in the first thirty seconds she is on tape. The children shout it across the yard. It is on the cut of the wedding, twice, in the singing. It is a completely ordinary word — you would say it to a plumber — and it means guest, and there is no reason on earth for anybody to hear anything else in it, and she wrote in her notebook on the first night that they were a hospitable people who used the polite forms.
They were not being polite.
They were telling her, ninety-one times, in a word she knew, what she was.

I do not know what to do with that. I have tried to make it mean that they were mocking her and it will not hold — there is no mockery anywhere in that sound. I have tried to make it mean nothing, coincidence, a language having one word for two things, and it will not hold either, because on the raw reel of the wedding a woman says it while looking directly into the lens and then laughs, and everybody around her laughs, and the laugh is warm.
The nearest I can get is this, and it took me until August.
They did not think she was the Guest.
They thought the Guest had come.
SIX OR EIGHT MINUTES
Twelve days is nothing.
Twelve days is a fortnight of somebody else’s weather.
I will go home with four hundred rolls
and a boy, and a reputation,
and for the rest of my life
when a room goes quiet
I will look at the doorway.
Day Six, evening, and this is the only time in twelve days that Parvaneh does it herself.
There is no footage. Jalil is asleep. It is in the notebook, on one page, and it is the reason I believe every other word in that notebook.

She writes that she went out after the Looking and sat on the low wall at the north end, near the poplars, because it was warm and because she had a headache and because she had spent the day asking eleven people about a garden and had frightened herself.

She writes that she decided to try it. She writes that she felt ridiculous. She notes that she had done a certain amount of this sort of thing in Tehran with people she describes, in a phrase I like very much, as serious about being serious.
She sat for what she estimated afterwards was between six and eight minutes.

And she writes — and this is the whole of it, and it is four lines, and she never told a living soul, and it did not go into any interview or any letter I have found in thirty-four years of a well-documented public life:

Nothing happened. I want that recorded. Nothing happened and I was relieved. And then when I got up my shoulder was wet where I had been leaning against nothing, and I stood in the dark and put my hand on it, and I have been sitting here with the lamp on for an hour and a half.
O. came out about ten and found me and did not ask. She said: it takes most people a year. She said it as a kindness.
I am not going to think about this. I have six days left and a film to make and I am not going to think about this.
I asked her who he is. She said: nobody has turned round in time. I said that is not an answer and she said no, and she went in.
That is the last entry for Day Six.
The next page is Day Seven, and it is entirely about lens choices for the bathhouse, and it runs to nine hundred words, and it is the most technical passage in the entire notebook.
I know exactly what that page is. Anyone who has ever been frightened at three in the morning and got up and cleaned a kitchen knows exactly what that page is.
PART FOUR — THE HANDLING
COUNTING HANDS
I have counted hands for six weeks
and told myself it is an editing exercise.
A man who counts hands is doing arithmetic.
A man who cannot stop counting hands
is doing something else,
and there is nobody in this building at two in the morning
to tell him which.
I started counting hands in July and I did not admit to myself what I was counting for until the middle of August.

It began as method. This is what I want to be clear about, because everything I did that summer had the shape of work and none of it was. When you find one deliberate thing in a film — the doubles, the retakes, the notes — the discipline is to widen out and look for others, and the widening is boring and slow and looks exactly like ordinary restoration. I was building a shot log. Setup, duration, subjects, coverage. Four hundred and six entries. Willem thought I had a grant.
And on about the fourth night of it I noticed that the boy is in the film thirty-one times.
Thirty-one. In forty minutes. Out of forty-odd children in that compound.

He is never the subject. That is the thing. He is not filmed once — not one frame in which the camera is pointed at him, not one shot that is about him, not one moment of coverage that anybody could describe as his. He is carried across the corner of a shot. He is in the third row at the back. He is at the edge of the bathhouse frame with his back to us. He is out of focus behind a woman’s shoulder, nine times, in nine different setups, on eight different days.
Thirty-one appearances, none of them intended.

I went through every other child in the film. The highest is a girl of about nine who is in it eleven times, and she is in it eleven times because she is bold and funny and follows the camera and does handstands, and Parvaneh clearly liked her, and she is the subject in four of them.
Nobody else gets past six.

I want to explain what that means to somebody who has not done this work. If a child appears in the accidental margins of thirty-one out of four hundred and six setups over twelve days, it is not because the cameraman liked him. It is because wherever the camera went, he was already there.
Which means somebody knew where the camera was going.

There are two possible readings and I sat with both for a fortnight. The first is that he was a curious, sticky five-year-old who followed the strangers around all day, which is what five-year-olds do, and which would produce exactly this distribution. That reading is good. That reading held for nine days and I was grateful for it.
Then I plotted the thirty-one against the shot log by time of day.

He is in the morning setups and he is in the late-afternoon setups. He is in eleven of the thirteen setups shot in the last hour of light. He is in none — not one — of the eight setups shot between one and three in the afternoon.
A child who follows strangers around does not observe a siesta.

I went and looked at what happens in this House between one and three. Nothing happens. It is the flat white hour. It is the hour when the whole place sits down and goes quiet, and it is the material she cut to three and a half minutes.
The boy is not in the Quiet.

He is five, and he is the only child in the compound who goes round at the Looking, and he has been given a token with a number on it, and he is in thirty-one shots he was never pointed at — and in the one hour of the day when every adult in that place goes somewhere he cannot follow, he is put away.
Not brought. Put away.

I sat in the cold room and worked out, on the back of a shot log, that if you wanted to raise a child inside a practice without ever letting him watch it being done, and then have him do it his whole life while believing it was his own idea, that is precisely how you would arrange his afternoons.
BEAUTIFUL THINGS
Name some beautiful things, she says,
and forty children shout at once
the moon, the sun, flowers, playtime,
and I have my hand over my mouth in the doorway
like a woman at a funeral
who has just been told a joke.
Name some ugly things.
And the room thinks about it properly.
Day Seven. The classroom. Two rooms, forty-one children, one teacher, and the light coming in from the left through windows with no glass in the upper halves.
Parvaneh gets eleven minutes of it and cuts four, and it is the four minutes that made the film immortal, and every word of what follows is on the reel.

Ozra teaches standing. She has an exercise book she never opens. She asks them arithmetic first and they answer it well, and there is a boy at the back who is quicker than the rest and knows it and has to be sat on twice.
Then she says: name some beautiful things.
