They go off like birds. All at once, competitively, over each other, the way children answer when the answer is free — the moon, the sun, flowers, the garden, playtime, my mother, God, the sun again, and somebody at the back shouts bread and gets a laugh.
Parvaneh is standing in the doorway with the camera running and her free hand over her mouth. Jalil has described her doing this to me twice and both times he described the hand.
Then Ozra says: name some ugly things.
And here is what is on the reel, and what is in the film, and what people in Frankfurt and Montreal and Bombay have sat in the dark and heard.
The room goes quiet.

Not shy-quiet. Working-quiet. Forty-one children think about it properly, and it takes four or five seconds, which on film is a very long time. And then a small boy in the front row says, without any drama at all, in the voice of a child giving a correct answer to a question he has understood:
Hand.
And then: foot.
And then, after a beat: head.
Nobody laughs. One girl nods.
And then Ozra says — and this is the moment the whole picture turns over, and it is why the film is what it is — she says: now make me a sentence with the word house in it.
And a boy near the window says the sentence that gave the film its name.
Four minutes. That is what is in the film, and it is perfect, and I have never in my life met anyone who has seen it and forgotten it.
Now.
There are eleven minutes in the trims, and the four in the film are minutes two through six, and I want to describe minute nine.

In minute nine the arithmetic is over and the beautiful things are over and Ozra has the children copying letters. The camera is at the back of the room on a wide lens because Jalil has moved to get the light. Forty-one children with their heads down. It is a static shot of a classroom and there is no reason for anybody ever to look at it.
Along the back row, behind the children, four adults are sitting on the bench against the wall.
This is normal. Parents come in. There are always two or three adults at the back of that room on any given day and they are in a dozen setups across the twelve days.
The boy is at the end of the back row.

Over the course of minute nine he is lifted by the first woman and set on her lap and she looks at his hands — palm, back, between each finger, the full sequence, exactly as it is done at the Looking — and she takes about forty seconds, and she talks to him the whole time, and he is bored and wants to get down.
Then she passes him to the man beside her.
Then that man passes him to the woman beside him.
Then that woman passes him to the fourth.
Four adults. Four minutes. In one static wide shot, in focus, in the background of a classroom, while forty-one children copy letters and a teacher walks between the desks.
I identified all four against the clinic sequence. It took eleven days.

Three of the four are among the worst cases in that House. Not the worst-looking — I checked myself very carefully on that, because it would be easy to select for the camera. The worst: the three whose hands and faces show the furthest progression of anybody who appears in the film, which means the three who have carried it longest and heaviest, which means the three most likely in that entire compound to give it to somebody.
The fourth is Golnaz from the kitchen.
He eats in her kitchen every day between the two firings, with the doors shut against the flies.

It is not cruelty. I need to write that down and I need to leave it standing. There is nothing in minute nine that looks like cruelty and nothing in it that is cruelty. The woman who has him first is delighted with him. She is talking to him the entire time and at one point she puts her forehead against his forehead, which is a thing my daughter did to my son when he was small, in a kitchen in Rotterdam, in 1988.
They loved him. That is not in tension with any of it. That is the mechanism.

You cannot do four years of this to a child you do not love. Nobody could hold their nerve. It requires, absolutely requires, that everybody involved be doing something they experience as tenderness — and the genius of it, if that is the word and I do not think it is, is that the thing they were doing was tenderness. There is no gap between the two. The handling and the love are the same set of movements, performed by the same hands, at the same time, and they cannot be separated by any method I know.
That is what has been screening at festivals since 1963.
FOUR FRAMES A SECOND
I have looked at this four times a second
for eleven days,
which is longer than she was ever there.
At four frames a second
a hand takes a very long time to arrive.
I have watched a woman reach for me
for eleven days
and I still cannot make myself flinch.

I ran minute nine at four frames a second for the first time on the ninth of August, at about eleven at night, and I finished at ten past four in the morning, and Els found me in the cold room at seven.

I am going to set down what that is like, because I have read a great many descriptions of people discovering terrible things about their childhoods and none of them have been accurate about the tedium.

Four frames a second is not slow motion. Slow motion is a thing you watch. Four frames a second is a thing you administer. You sit at a flatbed with your hand on the control and the image advances in small discrete jerks, and after ten minutes your eye stops seeing movement at all and starts seeing a sequence of unrelated photographs, and after an hour you are no longer watching a film. You are auditing.
So there is no horror in it. That is what nobody tells you. It took five hours and it was not a nightmare, it was clerical, and I made two cups of coffee during it and drank neither.
What I did was build a table.
Column one: the frame number. Column two: which adult. Column three: which part of the child. Column four: duration in frames, converted to seconds.
I have the table. It is one page. It sits in the drawer with the token.
Woman one: hands, both, palm and dorsum and interdigital, 41 seconds. Forehead contact, 3 seconds. Face, 12 seconds.
Man: hands, both, 22 seconds. Then he holds the boy’s right foot in his lap, without the shoe, for 74 seconds, while talking to the woman beside him.

Woman two: face and neck, 31 seconds. She wets her thumb in her mouth and cleans something off his cheek, which takes 4 seconds, and which is the single most ordinary gesture in the entire film, and which I had to get up and walk to the window for.
Golnaz: 90 seconds. She simply holds him. There is no inspection at all. He falls asleep against her at frame 12,433 and she sits there with him for the rest of the take.
Total: four minutes and eleven seconds of continuous contact, in one shot, on one day, of twelve, in the fifth of five years.
And at ten past four in the morning I found the thing I had not been looking for and had, I now understand, been looking for the entire time.
The wide shot has forty-one children in it and Ozra walking between the desks.
She never once looks at the back row.

Not one time in eleven minutes. And a teacher in a room with four adults sitting on a bench behind her class looks at them — you cannot not look at them, they are adults in your room, you check them the way you check a door you thought you had shut. She goes up and down the aisles. She turns at the end of each row. Her eyeline goes to the children, the window, the board, the children, the doorway where the camera is, the children.
Eleven minutes and her head never turns to the back wall.

That is not inattention. Inattention is random. Eleven minutes of a person’s eyeline never once falling on the four most conspicuous objects in her own room is work — it is as hard as anything an actor is ever asked to do, and she did it in a wide shot, cold, at nine in the morning, while conducting a class.
She was not avoiding looking at them.
She was avoiding drawing the camera.

An eyeline is a signpost. It is the first thing you learn in a cutting room: an audience goes where the people in the frame go. If Ozra had glanced at the back bench even once in eleven minutes, Jalil would have panned, because a cameraman follows a look the way a dog follows a hand, and there would be four minutes of coverage of what was happening on that bench, and the whole thing would have been on the record in 1963 in the most-watched documentary ever made in that country.
She held her eyeline off her own son of a colony for eleven minutes to prevent a pan.

Els came up at seven with tea and found me sitting in front of a frozen frame of a classroom with a page of arithmetic in front of me, and she looked at the screen for a while, and she said: ‘What am I looking at?’
And I said: ‘Children copying letters.’

That is what I said to my wife. Word for word. Sixteen years, and a woman who is better at difficulty than I am, standing in a cold room at seven in the morning with two cups of tea, asking me the only question that mattered.
Children copying letters.

I have apologised for a number of things since. I have not been able to apologise for that one, because to apologise for it I would have to explain it, and every time I get near explaining it I hear myself starting to make the case.
STEAM
The steam takes the edges off everybody
and for twenty minutes in that room
there is no difference between us,
which is the only true thing I have filmed,
and I will cut it to fourteen
because the committee needs to be moved
and not undressed.
Day Eight. The bathhouse, and it is the hardest day of the twelve for her and the best material she gets.

It is a low domed room with a stone floor and two pools and light coming down through thick glass discs set into the roof, so that the steam is full of columns. It runs for the women in the morning and the men in the afternoon and the children go with whoever will take them.
She gets twenty-two minutes and cuts fourteen and it is the sequence people mean when they say the film is tender.

Bodies in steam. Backs being washed. An old woman having her hair combed out by a younger one, taking a very long time. Two men shaving each other, which is done there because a man who cannot feel a blade does not shave himself, and which she films in one unbroken take of ninety seconds — the concentration on the face of the man doing the shaving, the absolute stillness of the man being shaved. Someone singing three notes and giving up.

And the whole of it, every part of it, is also the Looking. In water, in steam, without shoes, with everything visible. It is the same inspection she filmed on the walls on the second evening; it is simply that in here it does not look like inspection, it looks like a bathhouse.
The boy is in eleven minutes of the twenty-two.

He is handled by six adults over that period, four of whom also appear in the classroom bench and in the Looking sequences. He is scrubbed and passed and lifted and dried and passed. He is entirely happy. At one point he is put up on somebody’s shoulders and paraded round the pool and there is a shot of this from below, through steam, in a column of light, that is one of the most beautiful images she ever made and that is in the film at seven seconds.
Parvaneh, on that day, in that room, does the thing that will define her afterwards.
She takes her shoes off and goes in.

Jalil has told me this twice and it is the only part of the story where he becomes difficult to talk to. She left the camera with him at the door and walked into the water in her clothes, and she was in there for the better part of an hour, and she was washed by two women and she washed one of them, and everybody in that bathhouse understood exactly what she was doing and why, and it was not a small thing in 1962 and it is not a small thing now.
It is the reason they trusted her. It is the reason the film has what it has. Every account of her courage rests on that hour and every account is correct.
‘She came out,’ Jalil said, ‘and she sat on the step in her wet clothes and she said to me: they are not contagious, Jalil, and I said, madam, we do not know that, and she said: I have decided.’

She was right, incidentally. She was right by a wide margin. Nineteen people in twenty cannot catch it under any circumstances, and an adult in a bathhouse for an hour is at essentially no risk, and she went to her grave nine years later without a mark on her.
The boy sat on the step next to her afterwards while she dried, and she put her arm round him, and it is on the reel because Jalil left the camera running on the doorway to get the steam.
Twenty-eight seconds. The two of them on a step. She is looking at nothing and he is picking at the stone.
It is not in the film. She cut it because she is in it, and she had a rule about that.
THE PRICE
The doctor is a kind man in a kind room.
The teacher was a kind woman in a kind room.
I would like somebody to explain to me
the difference between them,
slowly,
in a language with no future tense.
I have to put the drugs in here, because the chronology matters and because I have been avoiding it for four chapters.

I took them from the middle of June. Three of them, one of which turns your urine and your tears orange, which nobody had warned me about, and I discovered in a lavatory at the customs shed and had to sit down on the floor.

They work. That is not in doubt. Within about eight weeks the thing was arrested and by autumn the specialists were using the word cured in the loose way they use it, meaning that the bacterium was dead and everything from here is management.

The patch on my forearm did not come back. That is not how it works. The wire is dead; the wire does not regrow. I have a playing-card-sized area on the outside of my left arm that will be discreet for the rest of my life, and I have been told, and believe, that this is an extraordinarily good outcome, and that men who were born where I was born and found their first patch at forty do not generally walk away with a playing card.
I want to record that I was grateful for about six days.
Then I began to be unable to take them in the mornings.

Not a decision. I would like it to have been a decision, because a decision can be examined. What happened was that I would put the boxes on the table and make coffee and go up to the cold room and at eleven at night realise I had not taken them, and this happened four times in a fortnight, and I am a man who counts frames for a living.
The second thing was worse and I noticed it in August.
I sat down at the flatbed one night in the first week and could not get in.

That is the only way I can put it. The thing I have done every working day since I was twenty-three — sit, look, go down into it, come up four hours later — did not happen. I sat in front of a frame for forty minutes and it stayed a frame. And at some point in the second hour my hand went to my face, and I noticed it, and I put it down, and eleven minutes later I got up and walked to the window and touched the radiator.

I stood there with my hand on a radiator in a cold room at two in the morning and I understood that I had never in my life done that before, and I understood what had been done to me, and I understood in the same instant that it was being taken away.
I want to be careful. I have read what I have written here and I can see the shape it is making, and I am going to name it rather than let it work on you unannounced.

I was not being taken away from anything. I had a disease and it was killing the nerves in my arm and it would have gone on to my hands and my feet and my eyes, and a man in a kind room gave me three drugs and stopped it, and every single thing about that is good.
And also: for thirty-five years I could sit still, and I cannot any more, and nobody told me that was going to be the price, and if they had told me I do not know what I would have said.
That is the sentence I could not say to Els in the cold room at seven in the morning.
Not: something terrible was done to me as a child.
I have been given something back that I was never asked whether I wanted.
THE GATE IS OPEN
The gate stands open all day
and there is no guard on it
and nobody leaves,
and I have written three pages tonight
about how cruel it is to keep people in a place like this
and I will publish them
and be praised.
Day Eight, the end of it, and this is the smallest scene in the book and I have put it here on purpose.

Parvaneh is sitting outside the school in the last of the light with her shoes off, drying her hair, and Ozra comes and sits down on the step below her with an exercise book on her knees, and marks it, and for a while neither of them says anything.
Then Parvaneh says: ‘The gate’s open.’
‘Yes.’
‘It’s been open every day I’ve been here.’
‘It is not locked,’ Ozra says. ‘It has never been locked. There is a chain on the inside for the wind.’
‘Then people can go.’
‘People can go.’
‘Do they?’
Ozra marks two more lines and closes the book.

‘Eleven have gone in thirty years,’ she says. ‘Four came back. Three died in the towns within the year, which is what happens; the towns are not kind and there is no work for a man with hands like ours. Two we do not know about. Two are alive somewhere and one of them writes.’
‘That’s not many.’
‘No.’
‘Why doesn’t everybody walk out of that gate?’
And Ozra says: ‘Because out there you cannot hear yourself think.’

Parvaneh laughs. It is on the reel — Jalil is round the corner recording room tone for the edit and the two of them are just in range, and the laugh is on the sound roll, and it is a real laugh, warm, the laugh of a woman from Tehran hearing a country proverb she likes.
‘That’s what everyone says about the city,’ she says. ‘My mother says that.’
‘Yes,’ says Ozra.
‘And you’d tell me it’s different here.’
‘I would tell you,’ Ozra says, ‘that your mother says it and gets in the car anyway.’
There is a pause on the roll of about four seconds.
Then Ozra says: ‘May I ask you something, since you have asked me many things.’
‘Of course.’

‘When you are old,’ Ozra says, ‘and it is all much worse than it is now — and it will be much worse, because it is being built, I can see it being built from here and I have never been anywhere — when it is a thousand small hands on you all day and every one of them beautiful, and people pay money for the hands and thank the people who make them. When it is like that.’
‘Yes?’
‘Where will you go,’ says Ozra, ‘to be quiet?’

And Parvaneh Kamrani, who is thirty-four years old, who has six days left in that House, who will be dead in nine years on a road outside Tehran with a suitcase in the back, says the thing that everybody says.
She says: ‘I’ll manage.’
PART FIVE — THE ERRAND
ELEVEN MINUTES
Eleven minutes of a woman speaking
and I have run it a thousand times
with the sound off,
looking for a mouth like mine.
I did not look for a mouth like mine.
I looked for a face that wanted me,
which is a different search
and finds nothing.
The eleven minutes is reel seven and it is the most famous single take in the film.

You will know it even if you have forgotten the rest. A woman sitting against a whitewashed wall with the light coming from the left, speaking directly into the lens, without a cut, for eleven minutes and four seconds. She has no eyebrows. Her hands are closed and she keeps them in her lap and does not gesture once. She is perhaps thirty and looks fifty and is, in fact, twenty-nine.

Over her, in every print, in nine languages, are eight subtitle cards. Eight, in eleven minutes, which is almost nothing — long stretches of her speaking with no card at all, and this has been written about at length and admired. The prevailing reading is that Parvaneh let the woman’s voice work as music, and translated only the essential, and that the sparseness is an act of respect.

The cards say, in sequence: I ask for nothing. My life has been given to me and I have not asked why. There is a garden. I will see it when I am done. My son is well. God is patient with us. I am not afraid. Let it be as it is.
It is a prayer. It has been anthologised as a prayer. There is a choral setting of it by a Finnish composer.
I watched it for eleven years with the sound off, looking for my mother, and I did not find her, and I have already told you that, and I want now to say why.

I was nineteen when I started and I was looking for a resemblance. That is the entire method available to a boy with no memories: you look for a chin, a spacing of the eyes, something. And this is a woman whose face has been rebuilt by twenty years of the disease — the brows gone, the planes of the cheek heavy and coarse, the whole architecture altered — and there is nothing on it to resemble anybody. That is not sentiment, it is anatomy. I have since put a photograph of myself at forty beside a still of her at twenty-nine and shown it to two people who did not know, and neither of them saw anything, and one of them said, kindly, round the mouth, maybe.
So there was no resemblance to find. Fine. That is bad luck and bad method and I forgave myself for it within about a week.
Here is what I have not forgiven.
She is the only person in that entire film who looks into the lens for longer than three seconds.

Everybody else does what people do, which is glance at it and away, or ignore it, or perform slightly. There are four hundred and six setups and I have logged every eyeline in all of them. The average direct-to-camera contact in that film is under two seconds and most of it is accidental.
She holds it for eleven minutes.

Eleven minutes and four seconds of an unbroken look down the barrel of a lens, by a woman who spent twelve days arranging her entire day so as not to be filmed, and who then sat down against a wall and did that.
A person does not do that to a camera.

You cannot. Try it. A lens is a piece of glass and there is nothing behind it and the human eye will not stay there; it slides off, it goes to the operator, it goes to the person asking the questions. To hold a lens for eleven minutes you have to be looking at something through it. You have to have somebody in mind, and they have to be very specific, and you have to want something from them badly enough to keep your eyes on a piece of glass in a hot afternoon while your hands lie dead in your lap.
I looked at that for eleven years and I understood it as courage.

I got Firouzeh to find me a translator in the second week of September. Not a subtitler — a linguist, from the region, with the dialect, who charges by the hour and does not ask what anything is for. I sent her a sound transfer and a note saying it was eleven minutes of an interview from a 1962 documentary and I required a literal transcript with no smoothing.
She sent it back in nine days with an invoice and a short covering letter.

The letter said: I have done this as literally as you asked, which makes it read badly in places. I should tell you that this is not an interview. Nobody is asking her anything. She is talking to a specific person and she names the relationship four times, and I have not been able to work out from the material who she thinks is listening.
NOW I WILL TALK
She sat down against the wall and would not be moved
and I thought, at last, she has decided to trust me.
Eleven minutes.
I had two hundred feet left in the magazine
and I let it run out
because her face was doing something
and I have made a career
out of not interrupting a face.
Day Nine, in the afternoon, and it is Sanam who comes and finds them.

This is the reversal that Parvaneh writes about in three separate interviews across the following decade, always with the same emphasis, always as the moment the House opened: the one woman who had refused for eight days came and stood in front of her while she was changing a lens and said, in Persian, badly, having plainly rehearsed it: now I will talk.
They set up against the north wall of the school because the light is good there after three.

Ozra is not present. That is the fact that matters and it is the only time in twelve days it is true. Parvaneh notes it in the book without comment — O. at the clinic, back at five — and it is in Jalil’s memory as well: he told me, twice, that when they came to do the interview he looked round for her out of habit, because for eight days she had been at his shoulder, and she was not there, and he remembers the small physical relief of it, like taking off a coat.
Sanam sits down against the wall with her hands in her lap.
Parvaneh asks her the first question in Persian and Sanam does not answer it.
She begins to speak in Azeri, straight past her, into the lens.

Jalil says he waited for Parvaneh to stop it. Any director would stop it. You have a subject who is not answering, in a language you do not have, looking at the wrong place — you cut, you reset, you explain about the eyeline. Parvaneh made a small movement with her hand which he understood, and he has spent thirty-four years not being sure he understood it correctly, and he thinks it meant: leave it.
So he left it. Four hundred feet. Eleven minutes and four seconds, which is what a four-hundred-foot magazine gives you, and it ran out, and she was still talking.
When it was over Parvaneh got up and crouched down in front of her and said, in Persian, gently: what did you tell me?
And Sanam looked at her for the first time — not at the camera, at her — and said, in Persian, the only Persian she used that day:
‘You will know.’
Ozra came back at five.

Parvaneh gave her the sound roll that evening in the school room and asked her to go through it, and Ozra took it and sat with the recorder for about forty minutes with the door open, and Jalil could see her from where he was cleaning the gate of the camera, and he has told me that she made notes.
Then she came out and gave Parvaneh eight sentences.

I have the notebook page. It is in Parvaneh’s hand, taken down from dictation, and there are eight of them, and they are the eight subtitle cards, word for word, that are on every print of that film in nine languages.
Parvaneh wrote, underneath: Beautiful. Use whole take. Cards sparingly — the voice is the thing.

She never had it checked. There was no reason to have it checked. She had a translator she had worked with for eight days who had rendered forty other exchanges accurately and helpfully and in beautiful Persian, and who had never once been caught out in anything, and who was standing in a yard in a colony with an exercise book under her arm being helpful again.
And Ozra had, I think, about forty minutes with that tape to decide what to do, and what she did was not invent something.

That is what has kept me up. She did not invent a prayer. If you take the literal transcript and you take the eight cards and you set them beside each other — and I have, and they are on my desk — you can see her working. Every one of the eight cards is a real sentence of Sanam’s, lifted out and set down clean.
There is a garden. Sanam says that. It is on the tape.
I am not afraid. She says that too.
My son is well.
She says that as well, and it is the fourth card in the film, and it comes forty seconds into the take, and a hundred thousand people have read it as a mother’s reassurance from beyond a wall.
Ozra took eight true sentences out of eleven minutes and left everything that held them together, and the result is a prayer, and the result is also a lie, and there is not one false word in it.
WHAT SHE ACTUALLY SAID
I am not a good woman and I have never claimed it.
But I have never in my life
told anybody something that was true
in order to prevent them from understanding.
I would not have known it was available.
Here is the literal transcript. I have cut it to what matters, which is a thing I am aware I am doing.
She begins by saying who she is and who she is speaking to. That is the first thirty seconds and there are no subtitle cards over it at all.
She says: I am Sanam, daughter of Mohsen, of this house. I am talking to my son. You are a man now and I do not know your name.

She says it in that order. Her name, her father’s name, the house, and then the relationship, and then the thing that has taken the ground out from under me every time I have read it since September, which is that she knew they would rename me and did not know what to.
Then she says: They tell me you will see this. They tell me it will be kept and that you will find it. I do not understand how, but Ozra understands, and Ozra is not wrong about things.
Then she says: I did not agree.
She says that four times in eleven minutes. It is the spine of the whole take. She comes back to it the way a person comes back to the one thing they came to say.

She says: I did not agree, and I want it said out loud in the open air with the machine running, because when this is over everybody here will say we agreed. We did not all agree. I am against it. I have been against it since they chose you and I am against it today and I will be against it when I am dead.
Then, and this is card three in the film, she says: There is a garden.
In the film that is a woman speaking of paradise.

On the tape, what she says is: There is a garden and I have been in it since I was a girl and I will not tell you it is a lie because it is not a lie. I have stood by the wall on the left. I have never gone past the water. And I want you to know that I would burn it. If it could be burned I would burn it, and I would burn this house, and I would burn Ozra’s book, and I would take my chances with God about it, because a garden that costs a child is not a garden, it is a field somebody is farming.

Then there are about ninety seconds of something the linguist could not fully resolve — the recording is poor and Sanam is not composed — of which the clearest part is: four years. Four years I have carried you into that room and given you to them and taken you back. Nobody made me. There is no one holding my arm.
Then she says the thing that is card five.
My son is well.

What she actually says is: My son is well today. He is well this week. He is five and he is well and he will be well for a long time, and that is the cruelty of it, that is the whole cruelty of it, you will be well for thirty years and you will not know, and by the time you know it will be an old thing that happened to a child and there will be nobody left here to shout at.

And then, near the end, with about a minute left in the magazine, she stops and looks at the lens for a long time without saying anything — this is in the film, it is the famous pause at nine minutes forty, and it is used in three separate documentaries about her as an image of endurance — and then she says:

If you have found this you are already ill and I am already dead and there is nothing I can do for you. So I will tell you the only useful thing I know, and Ozra will hear me say it and she will not stop me, because she does not think you will believe me.
Do not do what they taught you.
You will want to. It will feel like the only thing that is yours. It is not yours. It was put in you before you could talk, and everything you have built on it you built on their ground.

Get up. Walk about. Be interrupted. Let your body pull you out of it every four seconds like a dog pulling on a rope. That is what a life is. I would give this garden and every hour I have spent in it for one afternoon of being pulled about by a body that works.
I am your mother. I am asking you for one thing and it is this. Be interrupted.
The last twenty seconds are her saying his name.

Not Dariush. She did not know that name and never would. The other one, the one they gave me in that house, and she says it eleven times, evenly, without weeping, the way you say a word into a well to hear how deep it is.
Amin.
I had never heard it. Nobody had ever said it to me in my life.
I sat in the cold room and listened to a woman say my name eleven times in a language I do not speak, and I got up, and I walked to the window, and I touched the radiator.
THE FIELD
I have counted the rows twice
and the arithmetic does not resolve.
There are more of them under this field
than have ever stood on it,
and the woman beside me is telling me
that not one of them died of what they had.
I write: fatalism.
I have a word for everything
and the words are all slightly wrong.
Day Ten, in the morning, and Ozra takes her to the graveyard because Parvaneh has asked four times.

It is outside the north wall, through a gap that has no gate, and it is the size of a football pitch and it is full. Low stones. No names on most of them, or names that have gone. Some of the older ground has been walked flat and is only recognisable as a graveyard because of the way people go round it rather than across.

They walk the length of it together, slowly, and Jalil follows with the camera and gets four minutes that will be ninety seconds in the film, and it is the only sequence in the whole picture that nobody in any audience has ever needed explained to them.
‘How long has the House been here?’ Parvaneh says.
‘Since 1938. This was a stopping place before. There was a water tank.’
‘Twenty-four years.’
‘Yes.’
Parvaneh looks at the field.
She does the arithmetic again — she did it on the first day, at the gate, standing in the wind — and it comes out the same and worse, and she says nothing, and they walk.
‘How many died of it?’ she says at last.
And Ozra says: ‘None of them.’
Parvaneh stops.
‘None?’

‘Nobody here has ever died of it,’ Ozra says, and she says it evenly, in the tone she uses for arithmetic in the classroom. ‘It does not kill you. That is not what it does. It takes the feeling out and then it stands back and lets the world do the rest.’
She points with her chin, without any drama at all, along the second row.
‘Burns,’ she says. ‘That one, and that one, and the two beyond. A woman who did not know she was sitting against a stove. A man who put his hand into a pot to find a spoon.’
Further on: ‘Feet. Four of those. A hole in a foot that nobody found, and it goes down and down, and by the time it is a smell it is in the bone.’

Then, near the wall: ‘That one fell. He was blind by then. He did not go blind from the disease, you understand, he went blind because he stopped closing his eye and did not know he had stopped, and nobody was looking at him closely enough that year.’
Parvaneh has her notebook out and is not writing.
‘Every single one,’ she says.
‘Every single one is a small thing that a body would ordinarily have shouted about,’ Ozra says. ‘That is what the field is. It is not a disease field. It is a field of people who were not told.’
There is a long stretch of walking after that.
Then Parvaneh says: ‘And there are two hundred and ten of you.’
‘Two hundred and ten.’
‘There have always been two hundred and ten?’
And Ozra says: ‘There is water for two hundred and ten. There is bread for two hundred and ten. The consignment is for two hundred and ten.’
She says it the way a woman says the price of flour.

Parvaneh writes it down. She writes it down as poverty — as the pitiful fixed arithmetic of a place that has been given a number by a ministry and has never been given a different one. It goes into the film as an intertitle. It is one of the four hardest facts in the picture and a committee in Tehran will read it in 1963 and vote money.
What she does not write, because it does not occur to her and there is no reason it should, is that a number which never changes is not a limit.
It is a rate.
Two hundred and ten people in a bowl of ground for twenty-four years, and a field outside the north wall that is full, and every departure followed by an arrival, and somebody keeping the count.
On the way back through the gap in the wall Ozra says one more thing, and Jalil has the camera down by then and it is only in the notebook.
‘You want to know how long,’ she says.
‘How long what?’
‘You have been looking at the field and wondering how long a person lasts here. Everybody does it. You are all very polite about it and you all do it.’
Parvaneh does not deny it.
‘Nineteen years,’ Ozra says. ‘From the first quiet patch. Nineteen years, and then something ordinary happens to them.’
‘How do you know that?’
And Ozra says: ‘Because I have been writing it down since I was fifteen years old, and there is nothing else to do here, and eventually you have enough of them that it stops being a guess.’
SIX WEEKS BEFORE
I have been in this room since the light went
and the light has come back
and I have not moved
and there is nobody left to be proud of me for it.
The rest came fast after that, and it came in the wrong order, which is how these things come.
Firouzeh had sent the film permit in June with the pharmacy schedules and I had filed it without reading it properly, because in June I was looking for medicine and a permit is administration.
The permit is dated the eleventh of January 1962.
Parvaneh Kamrani’s application to the Ministry is dated the twenty-sixth of February 1962.

Six weeks. The permission to film at Station Nine was issued six weeks before anybody applied to film at Station Nine, and it was countersigned by the attending physician, Meshkat, and it names the applicant.
It names her.
In January, before she had heard of the place.

There is a second document in the same file, which Firouzeh photographed because it was clipped to the first, and which is a letter from the Society for Assistance to the Ministry, dated December 1961, proposing a documentary film about the leprosy stations and recommending a director.
The Society had received, in November 1961, an unsigned letter.

I have it. It is one page, typed, no letterhead, posted from Tabriz, and it proposes that a film be made at Station Nine and gives four reasons why, all of them excellent, and then it recommends a director in a single sentence.
The sentence is: Kamrani would do it and no one else would.
That is all. No praise, no argument. An assessment.
I have spent a great deal of time with that letter and I want to lay out what it knows.

It knows she is available, which she was, humiliatingly, after 1960. It knows she is out of favour and that a woman out of favour will take a subject nobody else will touch. It knows the Society is looking for a film and has money. It knows, or has correctly guessed, that she is childless and had lost a custody case in 1959 that was reported in two newspapers and that she never spoke about publicly again in her life.
It does not say any of that. It says: Kamrani would do it and no one else would.

Somebody in a colony eleven kilometres past the end of the road, with one newspaper a month and no telephone, read the country accurately enough to select, in November 1961, from the entire film industry of a nation, the one director who would come, and stay, and film what she was shown, and go away with a child.
They did not hope a visitor would take him.
They chose a woman who could not leave without one.
The school register I got in October, and it is the smallest object in this account and the worst.

It is an exercise book. Firouzeh found it in a box of colony material that went to a provincial archive in 1974 when Station Nine was closed and demolished, catalogued as teaching materials, misc., unexamined. She photographed forty-one pages and asked, in her covering note, whether this was what I wanted, because it appeared to be a class list.
Four columns, in that small upright hand.
Name. Arrival. First Looking.

And a fourth column, ruled with the others in 1958 or thereabouts, in the same ink as the ruling, headed with a word that Firouzeh translated for me as ripeness and that the linguist later gave me more accurately as when it comes.
Twenty-two children. Twenty-two dates in the fourth column, and every one of them is in the eighties or the nineties.
Nineteen of them are guesses. You can see they are guesses because they are ranges of four or five years and because three of them have been crossed out and rewritten.
Three of the twenty-two children have a note beside the name.
Sent.
Mine is the eleventh line. There is no name in the first column, only the word Amin, which is not a name, it is a description; it means the one who is trusted with something.
Arrival: 1957.
First Looking: 1958.
When it comes: 1994–1998.
I found the numb patch in March 1996.
And the number at the end of my line, which I took at first for a class number and which is written in the same hand and matches nothing else in the book, is 2006.

Which is stamped on an aluminium token that has been in my desk drawer since I was six years old and which I have carried through four countries and two marriages and have never once been able to explain to anybody, including myself.
THE MUSIC
There is a drum and a reed and a girl in red
and every ruined hand in this house is clapping
and I am standing at the back
with my eyes going
like a woman at somebody else’s daughter’s wedding
who has understood, halfway through the music,
exactly what she is going to do on Thursday.
Day Eleven, and it is a wedding, and it is the best day of the twelve and everybody knows it.

The bride is nineteen and her name is Roqi and she has been got up by four women since dawn in a red so strong it reads black on the stock. The groom is twenty-two and is called Habib and is being teased so mercilessly by the men that he has stopped being able to answer.

They set up in the yard between the kitchen and the school. There is a tar and a reed and a drum, and a man who plays the drum with the flats of two hands that have no fingers on them and who is, without any argument at all, the best musician Parvaneh has recorded that year.

She films eleven minutes and cuts four and puts them at thirty-one minutes into a forty-minute picture, and it is the reason audiences leave that film in the state they leave it in. She knows exactly what she is doing. Put the joy last and the ugliness earlier and people go out into the street moved. Put it the other way round and they go out into the street uneasy, and an uneasy audience does not write cheques.
Ozra suggested the placement.

Not the cut. Parvaneh cut it herself in Tehran seven months later. But on the eleventh evening, sitting on the school step, Ozra asked her — mildly, as a woman who does not make films — whether the wedding would come early in the picture or late, and Parvaneh said she had not decided, and Ozra said: late, I would have thought. So that they remember the music.
And Parvaneh, who had been thinking exactly that for three days, felt the small warm pleasure of being agreed with by somebody sensible.

The dancing goes on until the light goes. There is a moment — it is in the film, it is eleven seconds — when an old woman with no hands at all is pulled into the circle by two girls and dances beautifully, holding her forearms up, laughing, and the whole yard shouts.
Parvaneh is at the back near the kitchen wall with the camera when she notices the thing she notices.
The bride has no marks.

None. Not on the face, not on the hands, and Parvaneh has been in this House eleven days and has developed, without meaning to, the eye — she reads a hand now in half a second, the way you read a face for tiredness. Roqi’s hands are the hands of a nineteen-year-old girl anywhere in the country.
The groom the same.
She asks. Of course she asks; she is a journalist before she is anything.
‘Are they both from here?’
‘They were born here,’ Ozra says.
‘Both of them?’
‘Both of them. Roqi’s mother is the woman who does the bread with Golnaz. Habib’s father is buried out there.’
‘And they —’ Parvaneh does not know how to finish it politely and finishes it anyway. ‘They have it.’
And Ozra says: ‘They were born here.’

Which is not an answer, and Parvaneh does not notice that it is not an answer, because a drum is going and a girl in red is being lifted onto a chair and somebody has put a bowl of sweets into her hands, and because the sentence sounded like a yes and was built to.
She writes it in the notebook that night, in one line, in the middle of a page about sound levels:
Bride & groom both born in colony, both affected, no visible signs yet — early stage. God. Nineteen.

Neither of them will ever leave. Neither of them will ever be examined by anybody who is not Meshkat. They will be married in that yard in front of two hundred people, and they will have children in that House, and their children will be looked at every evening by hands that go over them very carefully, and some of those children will go quiet by thirty and some of them will not.
And the ones who do not will be married to each other in the same yard, with the same drum, and everybody will dance.

The music is real. That has to be said and it has to stay said. Nobody in that yard is performing. Roqi is nineteen and happy and it is her wedding, and the old woman dancing on her forearms is not a symbol of anything, and the man playing the drum with the flats of his hands is simply the best musician in the province and knows it.

That is what is on the film. That is what four minutes of the greatest documentary ever made in that country consists of, at thirty-one minutes, where the audience needs it, exactly where Ozra thought it would go.
FILED, NOT HIDDEN
You will not be told.
You will be given a room, and a door, and a long time,
and at the end of it you will walk out
holding something in your hand
and you will believe you carried it in.
Here is the thing I have been walking around since October and I am going to put it down now in one place.
It was not concealed from me.
Every single piece of it was placed where a man like me would find it. Not a man — a man like me. That is the distinction and it is the whole design.

The film is in every archive in the world and cannot be destroyed. The trims came to me at nineteen through two lawyers, which means somebody arranged, in the sixties, that Parvaneh’s material would go to the child when she died. The permit and the pharmacy schedules sat in a ministry box for thirty-four years, in order, in the same file, waiting for anybody to ask, and nobody ever asked. The register went into a provincial archive under a catalogue heading so dull that it guaranteed its survival. Sanam’s eleven minutes are the most-screened take in the film and have been playing continuously in front of audiences for thirty-four years with the truth inside them, unsubtitled, safe.
None of it was hidden. All of it was filed.

And the man who would eventually open it had to be a particular man. He had to have the disease, so that he would begin looking. He had to have no memory of the place, so that he could not shortcut it. He had to be sitting in front of that film for other reasons, for years, so that the material would be at hand. He had to have a profession that consisted of looking at single frames for hours without moving.
He had to be the sort of man who, on finding a numb patch on his arm, would go upstairs to a cold room instead of to a doctor.

I have gone over this a hundred times looking for the place where it could have failed, and it could have failed anywhere, and that is not the point. There were twenty-two lines in that book and three of them say Sent. They did not need me to work. They needed one of the three.

Ozra is on the sound rolls saying it. It is not in the film — it is room tone, it is on the end of a roll, it is her voice in a school room to somebody I cannot identify, and the linguist gave it to me in November as an afterthought at the bottom of a page of transcript.
We are not in a hurry. Hurry is a thing the body does when it is frightened of something it can feel.
And what she wanted was not a carrier. That is where I was wrong until October and it is where anybody would be wrong.

A carrier is a patient. A man sent out sick and told he is sick goes to a hospital in 1975 and is cured in a year and tells the story of his terrible childhood to two women in his twenties and is interesting, and nothing whatever happens, and the House is a sad chapter in a book about public health.
A man sent out sick and told nothing goes numb at forty and goes looking, alone, at night, for eleven months, and assembles the entire doctrine himself out of primary sources.
And a man who has assembled a thing himself out of primary sources believes it in a way that no convert on earth has ever believed anything.
They did not send a missionary. I had that wrong too, for about a month, and it flattered me.
They sent a student. And they left the curriculum in nine archives, in order, with the hardest material last, and they waited thirty-four years for him to be desperate enough to read it properly.
And there is one more thing in the register and it took me until November to see it, because I had been reading the book as a list of victims and it is not that.
Twenty-two children. Three marked Sent.
Nineteen not.

I had assumed the nineteen were the ones who stayed and got ill and are under that field. They are not. I checked the fourth column against the death record Firouzeh pulled from the provincial office, and of the nineteen, fifteen were alive when Station Nine was demolished in 1974 and went out into the towns with everybody else, and eleven of those are alive now.
Because they never had it.

Nineteen out of twenty people cannot catch this thing. That is the number the consultant in Rotterdam gave me in a kind room in April as a piece of good news. In a colony of two hundred and ten people living on top of each other for twenty-four years it means something else. It means that at any given moment that House contained a substantial population of entirely healthy people who had been told their whole lives that they were ill and had never been examined by anybody who was not Meshkat.

And a House of the fully quiet cannot run. Somebody has to carry the buckets and work the ovens and dig out there and hold the mirror at the Looking. A colony where every hand has closed collapses inside a decade.

So they were kept. Married to each other in the yard, in public, joyfully, with a drum, on the eleventh day of twelve, at thirty-one minutes into the finished picture where an audience needs the music.

I have run those four minutes perhaps two hundred times since November and I cannot make myself dislike them. The bride is nineteen. The old woman dancing on her forearms is not a symbol of anything. The man on the drum is the best musician in the province.
They are the healthy stock and the wedding is the mechanism and it is the most joyful thing in the film.
I have not stopped taking the drugs. I want that on the record, because I am aware of how this reads and I am aware that a man who writes I want that on the record is a man who knows how it reads.
I take them. Most days.
PART SIX — THE GARDEN
THE SUITCASE
Twelve days, and on the last morning
I woke before the bell
and lay in the dark understanding perfectly
that I was going to do it,
and that I would spend the rest of my life
calling it a decision.
Day Twelve. The morning.

The car is coming at eleven. Jalil is packing the cases in the yard and Parvaneh has been up since five, and she has written four pages in the notebook, and I have read them more times than is good for me.
The four pages are an argument with herself and she loses it on page two.

She sets out the case against, honestly and well: that she is thirty-four and unmarried and living in two rooms; that she has no money that is not somebody else’s; that she has lost one child in a courtroom already and knows what she is like; that she is a person who takes things out of places and puts them in films and this would be the largest such taking of her life; that the boy has a mother.
That last one is one line. He has a mother here. She does not develop it.

And then the case for, which is one paragraph and which is not an argument at all, and which reads: I have been in this house eleven days and I have not been able to sleep and I do not want to go back to my life. I am not taking him for his sake. I am not going to write down that I am. Whatever this is, it is mine, and I will pay for it, and it is the first thing I have wanted since 1959 that has nothing to do with anybody’s opinion of me.
Which is, I think, the most honest paragraph any adult has ever written about me.
The suitcase was packed on Day Four.

Firouzeh found the requisition. It is a colony supply note, in the small upright hand, dated the fourth day of Parvaneh’s twelve, and it lists one child’s clothing set, one pair of shoes to be obtained from the town, and travel documentation to be prepared.
Four days in.
Parvaneh spent seven more nights believing she was making up her mind.
The gate at eleven, and the car turning in the yard, and the whole House out for it, which she took as affection and which was attendance.

Jalil filmed the departure from behind because it was the only place to stand. That is the shot: the boy walking out through the gate towards the camera, with the wall behind him and the poplars behind that, and the light coming from the left. It is on the poster. It is the last image of the film and it is followed by four seconds of the gate and then black.
Sanam is not in the frame.
I have looked for her in every foot of that morning and she is not in any of it, and for a long time I assumed she had been kept away, and I built quite a lot on that assumption.
She was not kept away.

There is a wide shot at the end of the trims, forty seconds, panning across the yard while the car turns, and at the left-hand edge, on the roof of the kitchen where the women go to hang things, there is a figure standing quite still.
You cannot identify her. It is eleven frames and she is a hundred feet away and out of focus and the film is thirty-four years old.
But there is nobody else in that compound who would be on a roof at eleven in the morning on the day the House got what it had spent five years arranging.
She stood where she could see and where she would not be in it.
And that is the last of her. Eleven frames on the edge of a discarded pan, at the far end of a roof, watching a car go out through a gate that was never locked.

She died in 1968. Firouzeh got the record. It does not say of what and there is no grave number, because Station Nine was demolished in 1974 and the ground was cleared, and there is a state agricultural depot on it now with a concrete apron and a weighbridge, and I have seen a photograph.
I have a mother who spoke to me for eleven minutes and four seconds, in perfect confidence that I would one day be sitting exactly where I am sitting.

She was right about all of it. She was right about the House, she was right about Ozra, she was right about the thirty years and the numbness and the old thing that happened to a child with nobody left to shout at.
And she asked me for one thing.
I have not been able to do it.
MOST DAYS
I have been careful all my life
and it has made no difference.
The cold season does not arrive.
It is simply the weather
in a house you were born inside.
I told Els in November, in the kitchen, on a Tuesday, badly.

I had rehearsed four versions and used none of them. What came out was the medical part first, in the wrong order, starting with the good news so that she spent the first ninety seconds not understanding that there was any bad news, and then having to reassemble the whole thing backwards while I kept talking.
She let me finish. She has always let me finish; it is one of the two or three things about her that I have never deserved.
Then she said: ‘Since March.’
‘Yes.’
‘You have known since March and you have been taking pills in this house since June.’
‘Yes.’
‘Where.’
‘In the grey camera case.’

She went and got it. That is Els. She did not shout and she did not weep, she went upstairs and came down with the case and put it on the table between us and opened it, and there were the three boxes, and one of them was nearly full, and she looked at that one for a long time.
‘This one you are not taking,’ she said.
‘I take them most days.’
‘Dariush.’
‘Most days.’
And she said the thing that I have thought about more than anything anybody has said to me in sixteen years. She said: ‘Do you want to be ill?’
And I said no, and it was true, and it was not an answer, and she knew it was not an answer, and she sat down.

I gave her the rest of it over about four hours. The doubles. The cabinet and the fifth of a dose. The classroom at four frames a second. The eleven minutes and what is actually in them. The register with its fourth column and my line in it.

She is a sound editor. She has spent twenty-five years listening to things nobody else in the room can hear, and she listened to all of it without once asking me to slow down, and at the end of it she said:
‘Play me the eleven minutes.’

So we went up to the cold room at one in the morning and I ran the sound roll with the linguist’s transcript on the bench beside her, and she read it while she listened, and she does not have a word of the language.
At the end she said: ‘She is not talking to a camera.’
‘No.’
‘She is talking to you. She knows exactly where you are sitting.’ And then, after a while: ‘She sounds like somebody leaving a message on a machine that has not been invented yet.’

Els asked the practical questions after that, in order, the way she asks about a mix. Was I infectious now — no, not within days of starting the drugs, and probably not for years before. Had a doctor said that or had I read it — a doctor, twice, and I made him say it twice. Could it be passed to the children now — no. Could it have been passed to the children before — and this is where I stopped talking.
‘Before,’ she said. ‘When.’
‘Any time in the last thirty-eight years.’
‘And how would we know.’
‘We would not,’ I said. ‘Not for years. There is no test that reaches backwards. You do not find out until somebody goes numb.’

She sat in the cold room with the transcript on her knees and the flatbed humming and she said: ‘Then we get them tested and we stop thinking about it,’ which is the sanest sentence anybody has said in this account, and we did get them tested, and both were clear, and it means very little, and she knows it means very little, and she has decided to behave as though it does not.
I have watched her decide that. It costs her about a minute every morning. I can see it happen at the sink.
That is a kind of courage I do not have and cannot learn, and it is the closest thing to what Sanam asked me for that I have ever seen a person do.
FOUR THOUSAND TIMES
The children are asleep upstairs.
The house makes its four noises.
I have everything a man could want
and a page of arithmetic in a drawer
and I have been sitting here since ten
teaching myself not to go
and going.
The thing I have not written down is that I have been doing it all along.
I want to put it here, at the end, where it belongs, rather than earlier where it would have been a clue.

I have sat still every day of my life. Before the film, before the trims, before March. At twenty-three in a rented room in Utrecht with a dead job in a warehouse, at thirty in this house before the children were born, at forty in a cold room at two in the morning with an arm that had stopped reporting. Twenty minutes, half an hour. I never called it anything. If anybody had asked I would have said I was thinking, and that would have been a lie, but not a deliberate one, because there is no word available in any language I have.
And I have been in the garden approximately four thousand times.
Dry. Walled. A watercourse down the middle in a stone channel with the lip rounded. Something red at the far end that I have never got close to.

I have never once thought it was strange. That is what I need somebody to understand. It is not a vision and it does not arrive; it is simply where I am when I am not anywhere. Everybody has somewhere. I assumed everybody had somewhere. In 1981 I mentioned it to a woman I was seeing — offhand, in a car, as small talk — and she said, that’s nice, mine’s a beach, and we drove on, and I have thought about that conversation for fifteen years.
Hers was a beach. She had made it up. She had made it up that afternoon in the car, out of a holiday and a photograph, the way anybody would if you asked them, and it was hers.
Mine is a real place with an inventory.
I stand near the wall, on the right-hand side. I have never gone past the water.

And there is somebody behind me. He has always been behind me. He is behind me at about the height of a hand on a shoulder, slightly to the left, and I have never turned round, and I have never in my life wanted to, and until October I would have told you I had simply never thought about it.
That is not true. I have known not to turn round since before I could read.

Somebody taught a five-year-old boy, in a language he no longer has, in a kitchen with the doors shut against the flies, that when you are in the quiet place you do not turn round, because turning is what a startled body does, and being startled is the outside world’s disease.
And he grew up in Holland and married a Dutch woman and had two children and restored film for a living and never once turned round.

That is what four years in that House bought them. Not a belief. A belief can be argued with. They put a rule in underneath language, where I cannot get at it, and I have obeyed it four thousand times in four countries without ever once knowing there was a rule.
Since the drugs, I cannot get in.

I have tried perhaps ninety times since August. I sit down and the room stays a room, and at eleven minutes my hand goes to my face, and I put it down, and at nineteen minutes I get up and walk to the window.
It is the only thing I have ever been able to do that nobody else could, and it was not mine, and it has been taken back by a kind man in a kind room who was doing his job well.

I am aware — I want this recorded, because I have been aware of it the entire time and it has not helped — that this is exactly what she said would happen. You will want to. It will feel like the only thing that is yours. It is not yours.
She was right. I know she was right. I have the transcript on my desk.
And it is a quarter past one in the morning and I have been sitting in this chair since ten, not moving, teaching myself not to go.
THE OTHER SIDE OF THE BORING
Show me the child who can sit still
and I will show you
what was done to her,
and by whom,
and with what love,
and how long they were prepared to wait.
Bahar is fourteen and does not like me at the moment, which the books say is correct and on schedule.

She is good at everything in a way that alarms her teachers. There was a parents’ evening in October where a woman who teaches her physics told us that Bahar’s capacity for sustained concentration was, and I am quoting, not normal for the age group, and Els laughed and said she gets it from her father, and I sat in a plastic chair in a school hall and looked at the floor.
She revises with the door shut and no music. Kian cannot be in a room without a noise in it — the boy is nine and he is Willem, he is exactly Willem, up and down and touching things — and Bahar sits.

I taught her that. I remember teaching her that. She was six or seven and could not settle to reading and I sat on the end of her bed and said: do not try to make yourself. Just sit and let it get boring, and go through the boring, and there is something on the other side of the boring.
I remember being proud of the phrasing.
The other side of the boring.

I have thought since about where I got that. I did not read it anywhere. I did not learn it from a teacher. It came out of me on the end of a child’s bed in 1988 fully formed in a language I learned at five, and I gave it to my daughter, and she took it, and she has been going through the boring ever since with the door shut.
We had the conversation in December, on the fourteenth, at about nine in the evening, in the kitchen, while she was eating cereal standing up because there is no other way she is prepared to eat.
I asked her, as lightly as I have ever asked anything: what do you do, when you sit like that.
And she said, with her mouth full, irritated at being interrupted for something so stupid: ‘Nothing. I go to the garden.’
I did not say anything.
She said: ‘It’s a place. It’s just a place I go, it’s not a big deal, everyone has one.’
I said: ‘Describe it.’
And she put the bowl down, because something in my voice had changed and she is fourteen and not stupid, and she said, carefully, watching me:
‘It’s dry. There’s a wall all the way round. There’s water down the middle in a sort of stone channel thing, and there’s a tree at the far end with red on it. I don’t go down that end.’
‘Where do you stand?’
‘By the wall.’
‘Which side?’
‘Left,’ she said. ‘I’ve never gone past the water. Dad, what.’
And I stood in my kitchen in Rotterdam with the fridge running and my daughter looking at me, and I asked the last question.
‘Is there anyone else there?’
And Bahar said: ‘There’s a man who stands behind me.’
She said it the way you would say there is a radiator under the window.

‘He’s always there. He’s behind my left shoulder. You’re not supposed to turn round.’ She picked the bowl back up. ‘I don’t know why you’re not supposed to. You just aren’t. Can I go, I’ve got French.’
AFTER
Near the wall, on the left.
She has never gone past the water.
I have read that sentence in a stranger’s handwriting
and I know which wall,
and I know which side,
and I have known for a very long time
and have called it something else.
I have four things and I am going to set them down together for the first and only time, because I have avoided putting them on the same page since December and there is no longer any point.

One. Jalil, in Cologne, in June, describing a conversation from 1962: he asked a man in the House where a woman he had never met stood in the garden, and the man said, near the wall on the left, she does not come past the water, and it was correct.
Two. Sanam, on the tape, in the eleven minutes: I have stood by the wall on the left. I have never gone past the water.
Three. Me: near the wall, right-hand side.

Four. My daughter, in a kitchen in Rotterdam, in December 1996, thirty-four years after the film was made and twenty-two years after the House was demolished, having never seen the film, having never met a person from that country other than her father, having never heard the word: by the wall, left. I’ve never gone past the water. There’s a man who stands behind me.
Her grandmother’s position.
I have four explanations and I have worked on all of them and I am going to give them to you in the order of how much I would like them to be true.

The first is that I told her. Not deliberately — that I described it once, years ago, and she was small and absorbed it and rebuilt it and believes it is hers. This is by far the most likely and it is what any sensible person would conclude and it is what I would conclude about somebody else.
I have never described it to anyone. I described it once, in a car, in 1981, in nine words, to a woman who said hers was a beach.

The second is that it is a template. That a mind put into a certain state produces a certain kind of image, and that walled gardens with water down the middle are simply what human beings make when they make nothing, and there are pomegranates in half the poetry of that country and I am the daughter’s father and she has my brain. This is respectable. This is the one the linguist favours, gently, in a letter she did not have to write.
It does not account for the left-hand side.

The third is that they were right. That it is a place, that it has been there the entire time, that two hundred and ten people found the door to it because their bodies stopped shouting long enough for them to hear something, and that whatever is in it stands behind you, and that my daughter has been going there since she was six because her father put her on the road.
I do not believe this. I want to be extremely clear that I do not believe this, and I have written that sentence four times and gone back to it.
The fourth is the one I actually think, most nights, at about two.
That it does not matter which of the first three is true.

Because Ozra did not need it to be a place. Ozra needed it to be transmissible, and it is, and it has been transmitted, and it went across a generation and eleven kilometres and thirty-four years and a border and a language and arrived intact in a fourteen-year-old girl who thinks it is nothing and that everybody has one.
The fifth column.
I went back to the register in January and photographed it properly and had the linguist do the headings again, because I had been working from Firouzeh’s rough translation and I wanted them exact.
There are five columns. I had seen four.

The fifth is ruled with the others, in the same ink, in 1958. It has no entries. Twenty-two blank cells with a heading, and the heading is one word, and it is written in a slightly different pressure of the same hand, which the linguist says means it was added later, and which she translated as: after.
Twenty-two empty boxes, ruled and headed and left blank, by a woman who died in 1969 in a colony that no longer exists on ground that is now a weighbridge.

They were not aiming at a country. They never were. There is no version of this in which two hundred and ten people in a bowl of ground eleven kilometres past the end of a road expected to reach the world.
They were aiming at a household.

One man, one wife, two children, and whatever those children do. Small, slow, hereditary, patient beyond any human timescale, and — this is the part that I cannot get past, this is the part that gets me out of bed and walking about the house at three in the morning — indistinguishable at every stage from ordinary family love.
I taught my daughter to sit still on the end of her bed and I was proud of the phrasing.
I went back into the register one more time on the fourth of February, to photograph the fifth column properly for the linguist, and I found the last thing, and I have not slept properly since.
Three children are marked Sent.
I am the eleventh line. The other two are the fourth and the seventeenth.
The fourth line has no name at all, only a colony word the linguist gives as the quiet one, and an arrival of 1949, and a fourth-column date of 1984–1988.
The seventeenth is a girl. Arrival 1960. Fourth column, 1999–2004.

I have spent eleven months believing I was the errand. I have written that word down in this account more than once and I have turned it over and been frightened by it and, on certain nights, in a way I am not going to defend, flattered by it.
I was the second one.

There is a man somewhere who is roughly eight years ahead of me. He went numb between 1984 and 1988. He is fifty-something now. He was sent out of that House thirteen years before I was, by the same woman, with the same rule installed underneath his language, and if he is alive and if he did what I did — and there is no reason on earth to think he would not, because we were built out of the same afternoons — then he has had eight years.
Eight years of knowing.
And whatever a man does with that, he has already been doing it since before my daughter could read.
There is also a girl. She is thirty-six. Her window opens in three years.

I do not know their names. There are no names in that book. Ozra did not use names for the three, and I have understood since February why: a name is a thing that can be searched for, and she was not interested in three people. She was interested in three dates.
The fifth column is headed after and it is empty for all twenty-two.
Not because nothing was written in it.
Because it was not for her to write in.
NO EDGE
I am making a list of everyone I have touched.
It was going to be a short list.
I began it at the top of the page
with the two names that are asleep upstairs
and I have not been able to write a third
because there is no third.
There is only more.
I started the list on the seventeenth of January and I worked on it for eleven days.

The idea was containment. That is what I told myself and it is not a stupid idea: I have had this thing in me since approximately 1958, it sleeps for decades, it is passed only by long close living, and therefore the number of human beings at any real risk from me across thirty-eight years is finite and small and can be written on one sheet of paper.
I am good at lists. It is my profession. Four hundred and six setups, every eyeline, eleven days.
Here is what happened to it.

The first two names took no time. Bahar, Kian. That is the whole of the actual risk and I knew it before I picked up the pen — years of the same rooms, the same air, the same bedding, a father who has carried them and slept in chairs with them and been coughed on ten thousand times. Everything after those two names is arithmetic performed to avoid looking at those two names.
Then Els. Sixteen years.
Then my first wife, who I was with for four years in the seventies and who lives in Groningen and whom I have not spoken to since 1983, and who has three children by somebody else.
Then the woman in the car in 1981.
Then the man I shared a room with in Utrecht for nine months in 1979 whose name I cannot remember and whose face I can see perfectly.

Then Willem, who has sat four feet from me for eleven years in a cold room with the door shut and no ventilation to speak of, and who touches the radiator every eleven minutes, and who has a wife and a daughter at the university.
Then the entire second floor of the customs shed.
And this is where it stopped being a list.

Because Willem’s daughter comes to the building. She came at Christmas. And Willem’s wife works in a school, and my first wife’s three children are grown and have children, and the woman from 1981 was a nurse, and the man in Utrecht went home to somewhere in Friesland at the end of that year and I do not know where and never will.
By the fourth evening I had a page and a half and I was writing down a hairdresser.
By the sixth I understood what I was actually doing, which is that I was trying to find the edge of it, and that I had assumed there was one, in the way you assume a room has a wall even in the dark.

There is no test that reaches backwards. There is no year I can point to and say: before this I was safe and after this I was not. The thing sleeps for five years or twenty or thirty-five, and it woke in me in March 1996, and the only honest statement I can make about when I became able to give it to anybody is that it was some time between 1958 and now, and that nineteen out of twenty of them were never at risk from me at all, and that I do not know which nineteen.
I burned the list on the twenty-eighth of January in the sink, which was theatrical and which I do not regret.

Because the list was never the problem. The list was a man doing arithmetic at a kitchen table to avoid the two names at the top of it, and the two names at the top of it are asleep upstairs, and one of them goes to a garden with a wall round it every evening with the door shut, and stands on the left, and does not go past the water, and there is a man behind her.
And I cannot warn her.
I have tried. I have sat on the end of that bed four times since December with it all in my mouth.

Because to warn her I have to explain it, and to explain it I have to describe the House, and to describe the House I have to describe what they were doing and why, and there is no version of that account in which I do not, at some point, somewhere in the fourth or fifth minute, begin to make the case.
I know what I sound like when I get to Ozra. I have heard myself do it with Els, twice, and both times Els has gone very quiet and afterwards has been careful with me for a day.
They were not monsters. They had something. It was real and I have been in it four thousand times and there is nothing else like it and the world is getting louder exactly as she said it would.
That is what I would be putting in front of a fourteen-year-old.
So I say nothing, and she sits with the door shut, and I stand in the corridor outside it some evenings with a cup of tea going cold in my hand, listening to my daughter not making any noise at all.
The House is patient.

It has been patient for thirty-eight years and it can be patient for another thirty-eight, and it is not in a hurry, and there is nobody left in it to be in a hurry, and it does not require anybody. It is running now on its own, in a kitchen in Rotterdam, in a girl who thinks everybody has a garden.
I do not know whether I completed it.

That is the thing I will not be told. Not by a doctor, not by a test, not by anybody living. Whether I was the errand, or whether I merely survived it. Whether the man behind my daughter is a fault in a wire that her grandmother had and her father has and she has inherited along with the shape of her hands — or whether he has been standing in that garden the whole time, waiting for somebody from that house to bring him another one.
And whether, when I taught her on the end of her bed to go through the boring, I was being a good father.
I think I was being a good father.
That is the worst sentence in this account and I have left it in.
SUNDOWN
The bell goes and two hundred doors open
and the light is nearly gone
and there is nothing left to film.
Sit down. Take off your shoes.
Give me your foot.
We have a long time.
1962. The twelfth day. Four minutes past eleven in the morning.
The car goes up over the rise and out of the bowl of ground and the sound of it thins out and stops, and the dust hangs in the air over the road for a while and then that goes too.
Ozra stands in the gate until it does.
Then she turns and walks back into the yard, and pulls the chain across behind her out of habit, against the wind, because it has never been locked and there is no lock on it.

There is a great deal to do. The bench in the school room has to go back against the wall. The wedding things have to come down. Somebody has left a bucket in the middle of the north path and she picks it up as she passes and sets it against the wall, with two hands, and releases it.

The woman on the kitchen roof comes down the outside steps at about noon and goes in and does not speak to anybody for the rest of that day or, as it turns out, for most of the following week. Nobody troubles her. There is no one in that House who does not know exactly what she has spent five years doing and exactly what it cost her, and there is a way of leaving a person alone that is itself a kind of attendance, and they are very good at it.
The afternoon goes flat and white.
At one o’clock the House sits down.

Two hundred and nine people, on steps and low walls and in doorways, in the shade of the poplars and against the whitewash, and the reed-thin sound of somebody’s radio going off in a room, and then nothing. No one moves. A dog crosses the yard at ten past and lies down in the shade of the water channel and that is the only event of the hour.
They are all in the garden. Near the wall, along the left, along the right, in the shaded end. Nobody goes past the water.
Somebody is standing behind each of them.

At three the House gets up and the ordinary noise comes back — the kitchen, the school, a man calling to another man about a door — and the light lengthens and goes gold and then thin, and the poplars throw their long stripes across the roofs the way they have thrown them across the roofs since somebody planted them for the shade.
And at sundown the boy pulls the cord and the school bell goes.
Two hundred doors open.

They come out into the last of the light and sit down in pairs, on the low walls, on the steps, on the kerbs, in the same even distribution across the whole compound, husbands and wives and two old men and a woman and a girl and two boys who are told to sit properly.
They take off their shoes.

They take each other’s feet into their laps and begin to look — the sole, the heel, between each toe, the shoe turned over and shaken out and a finger run round the whole inside of it. Then the hands. Then the forearms. Then the face, with a mirror if both can see and with fingertips if not.
Somebody counts blinks.
There is talking throughout. Gossip, complaint, a boy asked about his arithmetic. It has exactly the tone of a family shelling beans on a step.
In the fourth pair from the poplars, where the last of the light is, a woman sits by herself for a while with nobody in front of her.
Then a girl of about seven comes and sits down in the space, and puts her feet up into the woman’s lap, and says something, and the woman laughs and takes hold of the ankle and bends close.
Above them the poplars move.
It is twenty-five minutes to full dark, and there is no camera anywhere in the province, and there will not be another one for as long as the House stands.
